meta.blurb: A driver takes a wrong turn in Sarajevo and stops near a young man with a gun. Within weeks, a promise from Berlin and a deadline for Serbia turn a crisis into a war much bigger than most leaders wanted.
meta.bible:
This book follows the July Crisis of 1914, from 28 June to 4 August. Europe: the Great Powers, in two camps. The Triple Alliance: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy. France and Russia had an alliance from the 1890s; Britain had friendly understandings (Entente) with both. Archduke Franz Ferdinand: heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, shot with his wife Sophie in Sarajevo, Bosnia, on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb aged nineteen. Franz Joseph: the old emperor of Austria-Hungary. Vienna: its capital. Belgrade: the capital of Serbia. Berlin: Germany's capital. Kaiser Wilhelm: the German emperor. Bethmann Hollweg: the German Chancellor. Moltke: the German chief of staff. Schlieffen Plan: Germany's plan to beat France fast through Belgium, named after Alfred von Schlieffen, and its exact rigidity is debated by historians. Tsar Nicholas: the Russian emperor; St Petersburg: Russia's capital. Poincaré: the French president. Viviani: the French prime minister. Sir Edward Grey: the British foreign secretary. King Albert: the king of Belgium. Liège: Belgian fortress city. Treaty of London 1839: guaranteed Belgian neutrality. Key dates: 5 and 6 July Germany's blank cheque; 23 July Austria's ultimatum to Serbia (ten demands, forty-eight hours); 25 July Serbia's reply and Austria's partial mobilisation; 28 July Austria declares war on Serbia; 29 July partial Russian mobilisation, 30 July general order, 31 July in force; 31 July German ultimatums; 1 August Germany declares war on Russia and France mobilises; 2 August Germany's ultimatum to Belgium; 3 August Germany declares war on France; 4 August Germany invades Belgium and Britain declares war. Words: Ultimatum, Mobilisation, Mobilise, Mobilised, Mobilising, Reservists, Chancellor, Envoy, Frontier, Neutral, Neutrality, Ally, Allies, Alliance, Balkans, Slavs, Telegrams, Archduke, Empire, Empires, Cheque, Garrison. Voice: calm, clear and fair; the book shows that nobody planned the whole war and that historians still disagree about blame. No invented dates, numbers or quotes.

Extended for the full-length book. Austria-Hungary: Conrad von Hötzendorf, chief of the army staff, long wanted war with Serbia; Count Berchtold, foreign minister; Count István Tisza, Hungarian prime minister, doubtful until 14 July, when he agreed on condition Austria took no Serbian land; Count Hoyos took the letter and memorandum to Berlin by night train on 4 July; Count Szőgyény, ambassador in Berlin, gave the letter to the Kaiser at Potsdam on 5 July; Baron Giesl, minister in Belgrade; Oskar Potiorek, governor of Bosnia; Bad Ischl, the emperor's summer villa. Archduke Franz Ferdinand, born 1863, heir after Rudolf (1889) and his father (1896); married Countess Sophie Chotek on 1 July 1900; three children; home at Konopiště in Bohemia, buried with Sophie at Artstetten. Sarajevo, Sunday 28 June 1914 (Vidovdan, St Vitus's Day): six cars, the archduke's open car second; about ten past ten Nedeljko Čabrinović's bomb bounced off the folded roof and wounded people in the car behind, he swallowed poison and jumped in the river and was seized; after the Town Hall the party went to visit the wounded; the driver took a wrong turn into a side street; Gavrilo Princip, born 1894, fired twice from a few steps away and both Franz Ferdinand and Sophie died soon after. Other plotters: Trifko Grabež, Danilo Ilić and others, seven in all; weapons came from Serbian army stores via Major Vojislav Tankosić and Milan Ciganović. Dragutin Dimitrijević, called Apis, led the Black Hand (1911), a Serbian officers' society; Young Bosnia, students; Bogdan Žerajić in 1910. Whether the Serbian government knew is argued; an Austrian report of 13 July found no proof that it did. Serbia: Nikola Pašić, prime minister; Prince Alexander, regent; the government moved to Niš on 25 July; Serbia mobilised on the afternoon of 25 July and Pašić brought the reply about ten to six; Giesl left Belgrade by train. The ultimatum had ten demands, among them Austrian officials working inside Serbia and sharing the inquiry, and the arrest of Tankosić and Ciganović; Serbia accepted nearly all and offered The Hague or the powers. Poincaré, French president, and Viviani visited Russia 20 to 23 July. Russia: Sazonov, foreign minister; Tsar Nicholas and Kaiser Wilhelm wrote as Willy and Nicky; Count Pourtalès, German ambassador in St Petersburg. Germany: Bethmann Hollweg, Moltke, Tirpitz, Zimmermann; Moltke refused on 1 August to turn the army east. Britain: Asquith, prime minister; Churchill; Kitchener; Grey spoke to the Commons on 3 August; Burns and Morley resigned; Prince Lichnowsky, German ambassador in London; Sir Edward Goschen, British ambassador in Berlin; Paul Cambon, French ambassador in London; Bonar Law and Lansdowne led the opposition. Jean Jaurès, French Socialist, shot dead on 31 July. Other dates: 24 July British cabinet; 27 July Germany refused Grey's conference; 29 July Austrian gunboats fire on Belgrade; 29 July Bethmann's neutrality offer; Italy declared itself neutral; Japan joined the Allies later in August; Ottoman Empire joined Germany in the autumn. Aftermath: Marne in September 1914; war ended November 1918; Versailles signed 28 June 1919; four empires fell by 1922. Names and places: Balkan, Bismarck, Dreadnought, Agadir, Panther, Alsace, Lorraine, Versailles, Trieste, Trento, Morocco, Victoria, Otto, Alfred, Tsar, Kaiser, Fischer, Yugoslavia, Luxembourg, Hague, Cuban, Marne, Liège, Portland, Scotland, Norway, Hofburg.

beats.scene: A sunny European street in summer, with horse carts and a newspaper seller
beats.summary: In summer 1914 Europe looks peaceful but its great powers are armed and mistrustful.

beats.scene: Holidaymakers stroll a seaside promenade while a steam train pulls into the station
beats.summary: Trains, steamships and telegraph wires have made Europe richer and more connected than ever.

beats.scene: An old veteran shows a child his medal on a quiet village square
beats.summary: The great powers of western and central Europe have not fought one another for over forty years.

beats.scene: A banker and a factory owner shake hands beside crates labelled for export
beats.summary: Trade and investment tie the great powers together, and some writers say war has become too costly.

beats.scene: Generals in plumed hats inspect long rows of soldiers on a parade ground
beats.summary: Even so, every great power spends heavily on armies and weapons.

beats.scene: A map of Europe with six large countries coloured in different shades
beats.summary: Six great powers dominate Europe: Britain, France, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia and Italy.

beats.scene: A globe with colonies in pink and blue and ships crossing the oceans
beats.summary: Britain, France, Germany and others rule empires across the world, and Austria-Hungary rules many peoples at home.

beats.scene: Portraits of three monarchs side by side in an ornate frame
beats.summary: The kings and emperors of Europe are mostly cousins, but family ties do not stop the quarrels of their states.

beats.scene: Crowds in a square cheer a marching band, with flags in every window
beats.summary: Newspapers and pride in the nation make people more willing to see other countries as rivals.

beats.scene: A calendar page for June 1914 pinned beside a map of Europe
beats.summary: This book follows the thirty days after the great powers made their fateful choices, and asks how peace was lost.

beats.scene: German princes and soldiers proclaim an emperor in a mirrored palace hall
beats.summary: In January 1871 the German Empire is proclaimed at Versailles after Prussia defeats France.

beats.scene: French families look sadly at a map with two eastern provinces shaded grey
beats.summary: France loses Alsace and most of Lorraine to Germany and hopes to win them back one day.

beats.scene: Bismarck, a heavy man in a uniform, moves small flags across a map
beats.summary: Chancellor Bismarck keeps France without friends by building alliances for Germany.

beats.scene: Two emperors sign a treaty at a long table covered in green cloth
beats.summary: Germany and Austria-Hungary sign an alliance in 1879, and Italy joins them in 1882 to form the Triple Alliance.

beats.scene: A young Kaiser with a short left arm waves from an open carriage
beats.summary: Kaiser Wilhelm II comes to the throne in 1888 and dismisses Bismarck in 1890.

beats.scene: A French officer and a Russian officer salute each other at a grand parade
beats.summary: Left without friends in Europe, France and Russia make an alliance in the 1890s.

beats.scene: A British minister shakes hands with a French diplomat in a London drawing room
beats.summary: Britain, once outside alliances, settles old quarrels with France in 1904 and with Russia in 1907.

beats.scene: A British general and a French general study a map in a quiet office
beats.summary: Britain promises nothing, yet its army and navy officers quietly hold talks with France about joint plans.

beats.scene: Two sets of flags hang on opposite sides of a great hall
beats.summary: By 1914 Europe is divided into two camps, and a quarrel between two countries might pull in all the others.

beats.scene: A map of northern Italy with small flags marking Trieste and Trento
beats.summary: Italy, the weakest member of the Triple Alliance, wants lands held by Austria and cannot be relied on.

beats.scene: Rows of young men in new uniforms line up outside a recruiting office
beats.summary: Most great powers train every young man for the army and keep millions of reservists ready.

beats.scene: Shipyard workers and cranes build an enormous grey warship under construction
beats.summary: Germany builds a great navy under Admiral Tirpitz, and Britain sees the danger to its sea power.

beats.scene: A giant new battleship with big guns slides into the water
beats.summary: In 1906 Britain launches HMS Dreadnought, a new kind of warship, and the race grows faster.

beats.scene: A tax collector counts coins while a naval architect unrolls a plan
beats.summary: The naval race costs huge sums and leaves Britons suspicious of Germany, whatever German leaders intend.

beats.scene: A German gunboat lies at anchor in a hot Moroccan harbour
beats.summary: Two crises over Morocco, in 1905 and 1911, bring Germany into conflict with France and push Britain closer to the French.

beats.scene: A German diplomat stares at a map with arrows on three sides
beats.summary: Germany feels surrounded by France, Russia and the British navy, and fears what the future holds.

beats.scene: A Russian soldier looks at a new railway line stretching to the border
beats.summary: Russia, beaten by Japan in 1905, is rebuilding its army and railways, which worries Germany.

beats.scene: A bearded old general draws a wide arrow on a map of Belgium
beats.summary: Count Schlieffen's plan is to defeat France quickly before Russia is ready, by marching through Belgium.

beats.scene: Railway officials in a dim room study a huge wall chart of train routes
beats.summary: Every great power has detailed railway timetables for moving millions of men to its frontiers in a few days.

beats.scene: Two staff officers shake hands over a war plan beneath a ticking clock
beats.summary: The plans of all the armies assume speed and a short war, which leaves little room for waiting or talking.

beats.scene: A map of south-east Europe with the Ottoman lands shrinking in shades of green
beats.summary: The Balkans, in south-east Europe, were ruled for centuries by the Ottoman Empire, which is now weak.

beats.scene: Villagers in colourful dress raise a new flag over a hilltop fortress
beats.summary: In the nineteenth century Greeks, Serbs, Romanians, Bulgarians and others won freedom, and Serbia became fully independent in 1878.

beats.scene: A Serbian farmer and a Russian priest stand together beneath an icon
beats.summary: Many Balkan peoples are Slavs, and Russia presents itself as the protector of Slavs and of Orthodox Christians.

beats.scene: Three students in a Belgrade cafe point at a map of Serb lands
beats.summary: Serbian nationalists dream of uniting the South Slavs, many of whom live inside Austria-Hungary.

beats.scene: Two capital cities, Vienna and Budapest, linked by a long river with steamers
beats.summary: Austria-Hungary is a patchwork empire of many peoples, ruled by the aged Emperor Franz Joseph since 1848.

beats.scene: An Austrian minister reads a petition from a crowd of villagers in dark coats
beats.summary: Austria-Hungary fears that nationalism could break up the empire, and sees Serbia as a magnet for its own Slavs.

beats.scene: Austrian troops march into a hillside town of mosques and church towers
beats.summary: Austria-Hungary occupies Bosnia in 1878 and annexes it in 1908, which angers Serbia, and Russia must back down.

beats.scene: Soldiers of four small armies march together past a ruined Ottoman fortress
beats.summary: In the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913, the Balkan states drive the Ottomans out of most of Europe and then fight each other, and Serbia grows.

beats.scene: A new border post stands on a Balkan mountain pass under a grey sky
beats.summary: Austria helps to create Albania in 1913 so that Serbia has no port on the sea, and forces Serbian troops to withdraw.

beats.scene: Smugglers carry crates across a river at night as border guards look away
beats.summary: Some Serbs, including officers, secretly encourage groups that train young fighters across the border, while the government hopes for peace.

beats.scene: A stern man in a feathered hat and uniform stands in a lodge
beats.summary: Archduke Franz Ferdinand becomes heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne after the death of his cousin and his father.

beats.scene: A young countess and an archduke sit together at the end of a table
beats.summary: Franz Ferdinand marries Countess Sophie Chotek for love in 1900, though the court thinks her rank too low.

beats.scene: A man and woman with three children walk beside rose beds at a castle
beats.summary: At home in Bohemia the couple live happily with their three children, and the archduke loves his rose garden.

beats.scene: An archduke at a desk reads plans for a new kind of empire
beats.summary: Franz Ferdinand wants reforms to give the empire's Slav peoples more say, which Hungarian leaders dislike.

beats.scene: A military adviser urges war while the archduke shakes his head
beats.summary: In earlier Balkan crises the archduke urged against war, so his death removes a voice for peace.

beats.scene: Teenagers whisper in a candlelit cellar beside a hidden stack of papers
beats.summary: Secret groups in Serbia and Bosnia, such as the Black Hand and Young Bosnia, call for Serbs and South Slavs to be free.

beats.scene: A letter with a wax seal arrives at a palace on a silver tray
beats.summary: The archduke is invited to watch army exercises in Bosnia, then to visit Sarajevo on 28 June, a day with a painful meaning for Serbs.

beats.scene: A thin young man in a worn coat reads in a Belgrade park
beats.summary: Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb from a poor family, joins the circle of Young Bosnia.

beats.scene: Three young men practise firing pistols in a park outside Belgrade
beats.summary: In Belgrade, Princip and two friends decide to kill the archduke and learn to shoot, with help from men linked to the Serbian army.

beats.scene: Three young men creep through a dark forest near a river border
beats.summary: The weapons are smuggled into Bosnia, other plotters join in Sarajevo, and by 28 June seven men are ready.

beats.scene: A railway station with bunting, a waiting crowd and an arriving royal train
beats.summary: On the morning of 28 June 1914, a warm and sunny day, the archduke and Sophie arrive at Sarajevo by train.

beats.scene: A line of motor cars with open tops moves slowly past a cheering crowd
beats.summary: A line of cars carries the party through the city, and the archduke's car has its roof folded down so that people can see.

beats.scene: Seven young men stand at spaced points along a riverside road in a crowd
beats.summary: Seven conspirators wait along the river road, each with a bomb or a pistol.

beats.scene: A young man in the crowd lowers his hand as the car passes
beats.summary: The first conspirators do nothing as the car goes by, one perhaps losing his nerve and another held back by a policeman.

beats.scene: A man throws a small bomb at an open car beside a stone bridge
beats.summary: At about ten past ten, Čabrinović throws a bomb, but it bounces off the folded roof and explodes under the car behind.

beats.scene: Police drag a young man out of a shallow river as the crowd shouts
beats.summary: Čabrinović swallows poison and jumps into the river, but the poison fails and the river is shallow, and he is seized.

beats.scene: An angry archduke in uniform stands in a grand hall with city officials
beats.summary: The cars rush on to the Town Hall, where the shaken archduke reproaches the mayor, then listens to the speeches.

beats.scene: Officers argue around a table in a hall while Sophie waits at the window
beats.summary: The party cancels the rest of the plan and decides to visit the wounded officers in hospital, and Sophie decides to go too.

beats.scene: A driver turns a car into a narrow street while officers call out
beats.summary: The driver is not told of the change of route and turns into a side street, then stops to reverse.

beats.scene: A young man in a dark coat steps towards a stopped car
beats.summary: Gavrilo Princip, who happens to be standing outside a delicatessen by the corner, steps forward and draws his pistol.

beats.scene: A car speeds through a narrow street as a crowd runs behind it
beats.summary: Princip fires twice, hitting the archduke and Sophie, and the car rushes them to the governor's residence.

beats.scene: Officers lift two wounded figures from a car in front of a stone house
beats.summary: The archduke and Sophie both die within a short time, before doctors can help them.

beats.scene: A young man struggles in the grip of two policemen as a crowd shouts
beats.summary: Princip tries to shoot himself and to swallow poison, but he is seized and arrested.

beats.scene: Police officers question a pale young man at a desk under a lamp
beats.summary: Under questioning, Čabrinović and soon the others reveal the plot, and the bombs are traced to a Serbian army store.

beats.scene: A wounded city street at night with broken windows and an angry crowd
beats.summary: In Sarajevo, angry crowds attack Serb shops and homes on the night of the murder and the next day.

beats.scene: An old emperor in uniform reads a telegram in a mountain villa
beats.summary: Emperor Franz Joseph, aged eighty-three, hears the news at his summer villa in Bad Ischl.

beats.scene: A German Kaiser on a yacht reads a message with sails behind him
beats.summary: Kaiser Wilhelm, at the Kiel regatta, hears the news and hurries home to Berlin.

beats.scene: Flags at half mast on a row of government buildings in a European city
beats.summary: The great powers express sympathy, but most people do not see a danger of war.

beats.scene: A grand funeral train and two coffins draped in black in a quiet station
beats.summary: The funeral in Vienna is simple, and the couple are buried at Artstetten, since Sophie cannot lie in the imperial vault.

beats.scene: A Belgrade street cafe where men read a newspaper with a black border
beats.summary: Belgrade expresses sorrow and promises to act against any Serbs who took part, but some Serbian newspapers write bitterly about Austria.

beats.scene: A general in a sash points at Serbia on a staff map
beats.summary: Austria's army chief, Conrad, has long wanted war with Serbia and sees the murder as his chance.

beats.scene: Count Berchtold, a slim man in a frock coat, stands before a map
beats.summary: Foreign minister Berchtold, who is usually cautious, decides that the empire must now show strength.

beats.scene: Old courtiers frown at a quiet corridor in the Hofburg palace
beats.summary: Many in Vienna fear that doing nothing would make Austria-Hungary look weak, and prestige matters to every great power.

beats.scene: A Hungarian leader with a heavy beard shakes his head at a council table
beats.summary: The Hungarian prime minister, Tisza, objects: a war might bring in Russia and Romania, and the empire has too many Slavs already.

beats.scene: Two Austrian ministers speak in low voices beside a map of Europe
beats.summary: Vienna knows that it cannot go to war against Serbia unless Germany promises to stand behind it against Russia.

beats.scene: A clerk seals a long letter with red wax at a candlelit desk
beats.summary: Franz Joseph writes a personal letter to the Kaiser, with a paper on Balkan policy that argues Serbia must be weakened.

beats.scene: A young count carries a leather case onto a night train in Vienna
beats.summary: Count Hoyos, one of Berchtold's closest officials, takes the letter by train to Berlin on 4 July.

beats.scene: An Austrian ambassador and a German Kaiser lunch in a palace garden
beats.summary: On 5 July, the Austrian ambassador gives the letter to Kaiser Wilhelm at a lunch in Potsdam.

beats.scene: A German diplomat in a frock coat listens to a seated Austrian visitor
beats.summary: Hoyos also meets the German foreign office, and hears the same promise: Austria should decide quickly.

beats.scene: The Kaiser listens to a general in a quiet palace room
beats.summary: Berlin sees the chance that Austria's strike may be swift and the war may stay small.

beats.scene: A chancellor in a dark coat sits with two Austrian visitors
beats.summary: On 6 July the German chancellor, Bethmann Hollweg, confirms the promise and tells Austria to decide quickly.

beats.scene: A blank cheque with an empty line for the amount lies on a desk
beats.summary: Germany does not ask what Austria will demand, and later historians call its promise a blank cheque.

beats.scene: Two grey shields with an eagle and a double eagle placed side by side
beats.summary: Germany fears that if it does not support Austria, its one reliable ally might drift away or fall apart.

beats.scene: A German diplomat pencils a note on a map beside the word Russia
beats.summary: Berlin hopes that a quick Austrian blow will keep Russia out, since the Tsar might not wish to defend killers of an archduke.

beats.scene: A thoughtful chancellor stands at a window overlooking a dark garden
beats.summary: Historians disagree about how far Bethmann and his colleagues expected a wider war, but they were ready to risk one.

beats.scene: A map of Russia and its railways with a calendar showing the year 1917
beats.summary: Some German officers argue that Russia will soon be too strong, so war sooner would be safer than war later.

beats.scene: A yacht sails out of harbour under a bright summer sky
beats.summary: On 6 July the Kaiser leaves on his usual summer cruise to the north, and other German leaders also go on leave.

beats.scene: A foreign minister in a Rome office reads a newspaper with a puzzled look
beats.summary: Austria and Germany do not tell Italy, their ally, what they plan.

beats.scene: A cheque book and a pen lie beside a sealed envelope in Vienna
beats.summary: The cheque binds Germany to Austria's choices, and Vienna now has freedom to act.

beats.scene: A calendar with July pages turned and a quiet street under hot sun
beats.summary: After 6 July nothing visible happens, but Vienna works on its demands, with seventeen quiet days before the great move.

beats.scene: Austrian ministers sit around a long table in a high Vienna council room
beats.summary: On 7 July the Austrian ministers meet; most want to strike at Serbia, but Tisza insists on demands first.

beats.scene: Farmers bring in the harvest with scythes while soldiers help in the fields
beats.summary: Many Austrian soldiers are on harvest leave, so the army cannot be ready to attack before the middle of August.

beats.scene: A pale official in a frock coat hands a report to a minister
beats.summary: On 13 July an Austrian official in Sarajevo reports that there is no proof that the Serbian government planned the murder.

beats.scene: Count Tisza sits alone at a Budapest desk with a letter
beats.summary: On 14 July Tisza gives way, after promising that Austria will not seize Serbian land.

beats.scene: A diplomat at a desk crosses out lines in a long draft and thinks
beats.summary: The Austrians write the demands so harshly that Serbia could hardly accept them all, and finish the text on 19 July.

beats.scene: A calendar with the date 23 July circled, beside a French flag
beats.summary: Vienna waits to deliver the note until the French president has left Russia, so that Paris and St Petersburg cannot plan together.

beats.scene: A French warship and a Russian palace seen across the Baltic Sea
beats.summary: President Poincaré and the French prime minister Viviani arrive in St Petersburg on 20 July for a state visit.

beats.scene: Strikers march along a wide avenue in St Petersburg past mounted police
beats.summary: While the French leaders are in Russia, large strikes break out in St Petersburg, showing that the Tsar has troubles at home.

beats.scene: A British cabinet meets under a portrait while a clerk holds an Irish map
beats.summary: In Britain, ministers are busy with a quarrel over Ireland and have little time for the Balkans.

beats.scene: A Serbian farmer carries a sack past a wall covered in election posters
beats.summary: Serbian ministers are busy with an election and expect trouble from Vienna, but not so soon.

beats.scene: An Austrian diplomat in a dark coat climbs the steps of a Serbian ministry
beats.summary: At six in the evening on 23 July, the Austrian minister Giesl hands the note to Serbia's government in Belgrade.

beats.scene: A list of ten numbered demands on a sheet of heavy paper
beats.summary: The note makes ten demands, and begins by saying that Serbia must publicly condemn anti-Austrian propaganda.

beats.scene: Newspaper presses stop while a secret society's sign is taken from a door
beats.summary: Serbia must shut down hostile newspapers and groups, change teaching in schools, and remove officers named by Vienna.

beats.scene: Two policemen with notebooks look for two men in a crowded market
beats.summary: Serbia must arrest two men linked to the plot, Major Tankosić and Milan Ciganović, and stop the smuggling of weapons.

beats.scene: A Serbian lawyer reads two highlighted paragraphs with a worried frown
beats.summary: Two demands go deepest: that Austrian officials should work inside Serbia and take part in the inquiry.

beats.scene: A large clock points to six above a sealed paper
beats.summary: The note gives only forty-eight hours, until six in the evening on 25 July, and threatens to break relations.

beats.scene: A young regent in uniform writes a telegram at a desk in Belgrade
beats.summary: The Serbian regent, Prince Alexander, asks the Tsar for help, and Serbia asks other powers for advice.

beats.scene: A German official at a desk reads a note and writes a short reply
beats.summary: Germany tells the other powers that the quarrel is for Austria and Serbia alone and that no one else should interfere.

beats.scene: Sir Edward Grey in a London study holds the note and frowns deeply
beats.summary: Sir Edward Grey tells the German ambassador that he has never seen such a harsh note sent by one state to another.

beats.scene: A Russian foreign minister bangs a table in a high-ceilinged office
beats.summary: Russia's foreign minister, Sazonov, is told that Austria is setting Europe on fire and asks for the deadline to be extended.

beats.scene: Russian ministers argue around a table in a palace on a summer day
beats.summary: On 24 and 25 July, Russia's ministers decide not to let Serbia be crushed and order the army to get ready.

beats.scene: Pašić and two ministers write a letter at a Belgrade table by lamplight
beats.summary: Back in Belgrade, Pašić and his ministers work on a reply, advised by Britain and France to be as polite as they can.

beats.scene: A train leaves Belgrade station at dusk carrying officials and boxes
beats.summary: On 25 July Serbia orders its army to mobilise and moves its government away from Belgrade, before the reply is even handed over.

beats.scene: A slim man in a black coat crosses a Belgrade square towards a legation
beats.summary: At almost the last minute, about ten to six on 25 July, Pašić brings the reply to Giesl himself.

beats.scene: A page of neat handwriting in French with a few lines underlined
beats.summary: Serbia accepts almost every demand, promising to punish and dissolve what Vienna has named.

beats.scene: A Serbian clerk points to two lines of reservation on a printed page
beats.summary: Serbia refuses only the demand that Austrian officials should work inside its borders, and offers to put the matter to an international court.

beats.scene: An Austrian minister boards a night train at a Belgrade station
beats.summary: Giesl declares the reply unsatisfactory and leaves Belgrade by train, breaking off relations between the two states.

beats.scene: A telegram clerk in Vienna rushes down a corridor with a stack of papers
beats.summary: Austria orders partial mobilisation against Serbia that evening, but its army will need weeks to be ready.

beats.scene: A British minister reads a Serbian reply and a pencil rests beside it
beats.summary: In London, Grey and others think that Serbia has gone very far, and that Austria has little reason to refuse.

beats.scene: Crowds sing near an embassy at night with flags and torches
beats.summary: That night crowds in Vienna and Berlin cheer, while the other capitals begin to feel the fear of war.

beats.scene: British cabinet ministers sit at a long table with Irish maps pushed aside
beats.summary: On 24 July the British cabinet spends hours on Ireland, and only at the end does Grey read out the Austrian note.

beats.scene: Four ambassadors sit around a small table in a London office
beats.summary: Grey proposes that Britain, France, Germany and Italy, who are not directly involved, work together to find a way out.

beats.scene: A German diplomat shakes his head beside a map in Berlin
beats.summary: France and Italy say yes, and Russia is willing, but Germany refuses, saying that it cannot put its ally on trial.

beats.scene: A Russian minister and an Austrian ambassador speak face to face at a window
beats.summary: Russia's Sazonov tries direct talks with the Austrian ambassador, but Vienna will not change its course.

beats.scene: Warships lie at anchor in a grey harbour as a signal flag is raised
beats.summary: Britain's fleet, gathered for a review, is ordered by Churchill not to disperse, a quiet warning to Germany.

beats.scene: A British ambassador and a French ambassador whisper in a corridor
beats.summary: France asks what Britain will do, but Grey cannot promise anything because his government and Parliament are divided.

beats.scene: A man in a London office draws a line under two columns
beats.summary: Some historians say a clear British warning to Berlin earlier might have helped, while others say it might have made France and Russia bolder.

beats.scene: A German ambassador in London sits stiffly across from Sir Edward Grey
beats.summary: On 29 July Grey tells the German ambassador that Britain may not stay out if France is drawn in.

beats.scene: Ministers in a smoky London room read newspapers and speak quietly
beats.summary: Most of the British cabinet still hopes to stay out of any war, and public opinion is far from ready for it.

beats.scene: Anxious people queue outside a bank while a stock exchange board shows falling prices
beats.summary: Stock markets fall sharply in many capitals, and people rush to banks for gold, showing that fear is spreading.

beats.scene: An old emperor signs a paper while a minister waits beside him
beats.summary: On 28 July Emperor Franz Joseph signs the declaration of war on Serbia, and a telegram carries it to Belgrade.

beats.scene: Austrian officials in a Vienna corridor study a wall calendar and a map

Fast trains took families to the sea, and news travelled by wire.
For over forty years, the big European armies had not fought each other.
Countries sold goods to each other, so many people said war made no sense.
Even so, every big country spent a lot of money on its army.
Six great powers led Europe, and Britain, France and Germany were three of them.
Britain and France ruled land far away, in Africa and in Asia.
The kings of Europe were often cousins, but they did not always agree.
Many people were proud of their country and afraid of others.
This book tells how that peace ended in only thirty days.
In 1871, Germany became one country after it beat France in a war.
France lost two eastern regions to Germany, and it wanted them back.
The German leader, Bismarck, made friends with other countries to keep France alone.
In 1879, Germany and Austria promised to help each other in war.
In 1890, the young German Kaiser sent Bismarck away.
France and Russia became friends and promised to help each other.
Britain solved old problems with France in 1904 and with Russia in 1907.
Britain made no promise to fight, but its officers talked with French officers.
Europe now had two groups of countries, and each group made promises.
Italy was in the German group, but Italy and Austria did not trust each other.
Most young men served in the army, then went home and waited.
Germany built many warships, and Britain felt afraid.

The ships cost a lot of money and made Britain and Germany enemies.

Germany felt that enemies were all around it.

Every country had a timetable for sending soldiers to the border by train.

B1B2: In the summer of 1914, Europe seemed peaceful and prosperous. Yet beneath the calm, the great powers had been arming for years and trusted each other very little.
Fast trains carried families to the seaside, and steamships linked the continents. Newspapers and telegraph wires brought the news of the world to a breakfast table within hours.
Among the great powers of western and central Europe, there had been no war for more than forty years. A whole generation had grown up knowing the army mostly as a parade.
Factories, banks and ships tied the countries of Europe together in trade. Some writers argued that a war between great powers would cost so much that no sensible leader would start one.
Even so, every great power was spending heavily on soldiers, guns and warships. Each said that it was only defending itself, and each feared the others' growing strength.
Six great powers dominated Europe in 1914: Britain, France, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia and Italy. They were the countries whose armies and diplomats decided what happened on the continent.
Britain and France ruled huge empires in Africa and Asia, and Germany had colonies of its own. Austria-Hungary and Russia had empires too, but theirs lay across the land at home.
Many of the rulers of Europe were related, and Queen Victoria's grandchildren sat on several thrones. Yet family ties counted for little when the interests of their countries pulled them apart.
Newspapers and school books taught people to be proud of their own country. They also taught them to see other countries as rivals, and sometimes as enemies.
This book asks a simple question: how did a peaceful summer turn into a world war in about a month? To answer it, we must first meet the countries, the promises and the plans.
In 1871, after a short war, the German states joined to form one empire under the king of Prussia. The new emperor was proclaimed in the palace of Versailles, in the heart of defeated France.
France had to give up Alsace and part of Lorraine to Germany. Many French people never accepted the loss, and they hoped that one day those lands would be French again.
Otto von Bismarck, the German chancellor, wanted Germany to feel safe. He made agreements with other great powers so that France would have no friends to help it.
In 1879, Germany and Austria-Hungary agreed to help each other if Russia attacked. Italy joined them in 1882, and the three became known as the Triple Alliance.
Wilhelm II became German emperor in 1888, when he was twenty-nine. Two years later he dismissed Bismarck, and the careful balance of the old chancellor began to fall apart.
Russia, no longer tied to Germany, turned to France, and in the 1890s the two countries made an alliance. Each promised to help the other if Germany attacked.

For many years Britain stayed out of the alliances that divided the rest of Europe. In 1904 it settled old colonial quarrels with France, and in 1907 it did the same with Russia, which brought the three countries closer.

Britain never promised in writing to fight for France, and its leaders said so often. Still, from 1906 its officers held secret talks with French officers about how they might work together if war came.
By 1914, Europe was split into two camps: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy on one side, and France, Russia and Britain on the other. A quarrel between two countries could now pull in all the rest.
Italy belonged to the Triple Alliance, but it was the least reliable member. It wanted some towns where Italians lived, such as Trento and Trieste, which belonged to Austria.
In most big countries, young men had to serve in the army for a time. After that, they went home as reservists, ready to be called back if war came.
Kaiser Wilhelm wanted Germany to have a great fleet, and his admiral, Tirpitz, set about building one. Britain, whose safety and trade depended on the sea, saw this as a direct challenge.
In 1906, Britain launched HMS Dreadnought, a battleship with big guns and great speed. It made all older warships look weak, so everyone began building new ones.
Warships were very expensive, and both countries paid heavily for them. The race did not give Germany the sea power it hoped for, but it made many British people distrust Germany.
Twice, in 1905 and 1911, Germany challenged France over Morocco in North Africa. In 1911 it even sent a gunboat, the Panther, to the port of Agadir.
Many Germans felt surrounded by enemies: France in the west, Russia in the east and the British navy at sea. Their leaders were afraid that Germany's time as a leading power would soon run out.
In 1905, Russia lost a war against Japan, and a revolution shook the country. Afterwards it began to rebuild its army and railways, and German leaders began to fear its growing strength.
General Alfred von Schlieffen, who led the German staff until 1906, planned for a war on two fronts. His idea was to beat France quickly, through Belgium, before slow Russia could be ready.
Every great power had a detailed timetable to send its soldiers to the border by train. Such plans were made long before, with every train, bridge and station worked out in advance.
All the plans depended on moving first and moving fast. The generals expected a short war, so they thought that any delay would be a dangerous mistake.
The Balkans are the mountainous lands in south-east Europe. For centuries they had belonged to the Ottoman Empire, but by 1914 that empire was weak and shrinking.
During the nineteenth century, Greeks, Serbs, Romanians, Bulgarians and others won freedom from Ottoman rule. Serbia, which had governed itself for some time, became fully independent in 1878.
Many Balkan peoples, including the Serbs, are Slavs and belong to the Orthodox Church. Russia, which is also a Slav country, liked to see itself as their protector and often helped Serbia.
Many Serbs dreamed of a single state for all the South Slavs, the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. But millions of these people lived inside Austria-Hungary, so the dream threatened the empire.
Austria-Hungary was a patchwork of peoples, among them Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Croats and Serbs. Its emperor, Franz Joseph, had ruled since 1848, and in 1914 he was eighty-three.
Many peoples inside Austria-Hungary wanted more rights, and some wanted to leave. Vienna feared that a strong, free Serbia would act like a magnet for its own Slav subjects.

Austria-Hungary had occupied Bosnia in 1878, and in 1908 it announced that Bosnia was now part of the empire. Serbia was furious, since many Serbs lived there, and Russia protested but had to back down.

In 1912, Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro joined forces and drove the Ottomans out of most of their lands in Europe. They then quarrelled over the spoils, and by 1913 Serbia had grown much larger.

The great powers helped to create a new country, Albania, in 1913, and Austria wanted it so that Serbia would not reach the sea. In October, an Austrian warning forced Serbian troops to leave Albania.
In Serbia, patriotic groups and some army officers secretly helped young men who wanted to fight Austrian rule. The government of Prime Minister Pašić, tired after two wars, wanted peace.
Franz Ferdinand was not born to be the next emperor. He became the heir after the sad death of his cousin Rudolf in 1889 and the death of his own father in 1896.
Franz Ferdinand married Sophie Chotek, a Bohemian countess, in 1900. The court thought her rank too low for a future emperor, so their children could never inherit the throne.
At home in the castle of Konopiště, in Bohemia, the couple lived quietly with their three children. The archduke was a keen hunter, and he was also proud of his rose garden.
Franz Ferdinand believed that the empire must give its Slav peoples a bigger voice if it wanted to survive. Many Hungarian leaders disliked this idea because it would reduce their own power.
In earlier crises, several generals asked for a war against Serbia. Franz Ferdinand did not, as he feared that a war could destroy the empire, and so his death took away a voice for peace.

The Black Hand was a secret society of Serbian officers, formed in 1911, whose leader was called Apis. In Bosnia, a group of young people known as Young Bosnia admired men who had given their lives against Austria.
In June 1914, the archduke went to Bosnia to watch army exercises, and he planned a visit to Sarajevo on 28 June. This date, St Vitus's Day, is the anniversary of a famous Serb defeat in 1389.

Gavrilo Princip was born in 1894 to a poor Serb family in the hills of Bosnia. Thin, serious and fond of poetry, he left school in Sarajevo and went to Belgrade, where he joined other young nationalists.
In the spring of 1914, Princip and two friends in Belgrade decided to kill the archduke on his visit. Some men linked to the Serbian army gave them pistols and bombs and taught them how to shoot.

In the weeks before the visit, the young men crossed into Bosnia with their weapons, helped by smugglers and border guards. In Sarajevo, others joined them, and by 28 June there were seven men ready to act.

On the sunny morning of 28 June 1914, the archduke and Sophie travelled by train from the spa town of Ilidža into Sarajevo. The city had decorated its streets with flags, and many people had come out to see them.
A line of six cars set out along the river road. The roof of the archduke's car was folded down, so that the crowds could see the royal couple clearly.
Seven young men stood in the crowd at different points along the river road. Each one carried a bomb or a pistol, and each hoped for a chance to strike.
As the car passed the first men, nothing happened. According to later accounts, one lost his nerve and another found a policeman standing close beside him.
Near a bridge, Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a bomb at the archduke's car at about ten past ten. It bounced off the folded roof and exploded under the car behind, wounding several people.
Čabrinović swallowed a pill of poison and jumped into the river. The poison was old and did not kill him, and the water was so low in summer that the police quickly caught him.
The cars drove on quickly to the Town Hall. There the archduke told the mayor, with anger, that he had come as a guest and had been greeted with bombs.
After the speeches, the archduke wanted to visit the wounded officers in hospital. Sophie said that she would go with him, and nobody believed that a second attack was likely.
Nobody had told the driver about the change of route, and he turned right into a narrow side street. The governor shouted that this was the wrong way, and the driver stopped the car to reverse.
By chance, Gavrilo Princip was standing outside a delicatessen near the corner, only a few steps from the stopped car. He saw the royal couple, stepped forward and drew his pistol.

Princip stepped forward and fired twice into the car, hitting both people sitting in it. One bullet hit the archduke in the neck, and the other struck Sophie, and the driver sped away towards the governor's residence.
The archduke and his wife were carried into the governor's residence. Within a short time, both of them had died, and the doctors could do nothing to save them.
Princip tried to turn his pistol on himself, and he also swallowed poison. Both attempts failed, and the police seized him before an angry crowd could hurt him further.
The police questioned the prisoners, and within days they had found the other plotters. The bombs, they learned, came from a Serbian army store, and the young men had been helped to cross the border.
That evening and the next day, angry crowds attacked the shops and homes of Serbs in Sarajevo. The police did little to stop them for many hours.
The old Emperor Franz Joseph was at his summer villa in Bad Ischl when the news arrived. He was shocked by the murder, though he had never been close to his nephew.
Kaiser Wilhelm was sailing at the Kiel regatta when he heard the news. He was upset, because he had admired the archduke, and he went home to Berlin at once.
Across Europe, flags were lowered and kings and presidents sent messages of sympathy. Most people felt shock, but few of them thought that the murder would lead to a war between the great powers.

The funeral in Vienna was held in early July, and it was quieter than usual for an heir to the throne. The couple were buried at Artstetten castle, because Sophie could not lie in the imperial family's vault.
The Serbian government said that it was sorry and would punish any guilty Serbs. But some newspapers in Belgrade wrote bitterly about Austria, and that angered Vienna still more.
General Conrad, the chief of the Austrian army staff, had urged war against Serbia many times. The old emperor had always refused, but now the murder gave Conrad a stronger argument.
Count Berchtold, the foreign minister, was usually cautious and slow to decide. This time, however, he thought that Austria must show strength, or lose its place as a great power.
Many in Vienna feared that if they did nothing, Austria-Hungary would look weak. For a great power, such a loss of respect was almost as worrying as a defeat in battle.
Count Tisza, the prime minister of Hungary, did not want to attack Serbia. He feared that a war might bring in Russia and Romania, and that the empire would only gain more unhappy Slavs.
Austria-Hungary knew very well that Russia might come to the defence of Serbia. It could not risk a war against both of them unless Germany promised to stand behind it.
Emperor Franz Joseph wrote a letter to Kaiser Wilhelm. With it came a paper on Balkan policy, written before the murder, which argued that Serbia must be weakened as a power.
Count Alexander Hoyos, a young official who worked closely with Berchtold, was chosen to take the letter to Berlin. He left Vienna by night train on 4 July, with the papers in a locked case.

On 5 July, the Austrian ambassador, Count Szőgyény, gave the letter to Kaiser Wilhelm at the New Palace in Potsdam. The Kaiser read it carefully and said that he would give his answer after talking with the Chancellor.
Meanwhile, Count Hoyos talked with senior officials in the German foreign office. They too promised their support, and they added that Austria should act quickly if it meant to act at all.
In Berlin, many officials hoped that Austria could strike swiftly, and that the war would stay small. They also knew that if Russia joined in, the danger would be much greater.
On 6 July, the German chancellor, Bethmann Hollweg, met the Austrian visitors and repeated the Kaiser's promise. He told them that Austria should decide for itself, and that it should not delay.
Germany did not ask what Austria planned to demand from Serbia, or what it would do next. Historians later called the promise a blank cheque, because Austria could fill in any amount.
Germany had few reliable friends, and Austria-Hungary was the most important one. If Berlin refused to help, German leaders feared, Vienna might turn away or even fall apart.
German leaders hoped that Russia would stay out of a quarrel over the murder of an archduke. They thought that the Tsar, a ruler himself, would not wish to defend men who killed royalty.
Historians still disagree about how much the German leaders wanted a bigger war. What seems clear is that they did not rule one out, and that they were ready to take the risk.
Some German officers believed that Russia was growing stronger every year. They argued that if war had to come, it would be safer to fight in 1914 than in 1917.
On 6 July, Kaiser Wilhelm left on his usual summer cruise in the far north. Several other senior officials and officers also went away on leave in the following days.
Austria and Germany did not tell Italy, their third partner, about the plan. The Italians would only learn of it when it was nearly too late to have any say.
With the promise in hand, Vienna was free to choose. But Germany had tied itself to whatever Austria decided to do next.
After 6 July, almost nothing seemed to happen in the open. Behind closed doors, however, Vienna was working on its demands for Serbia.
On 7 July, the Austrian ministers met in Vienna to decide what to do. Most of them wanted to strike at Serbia, but Tisza insisted that the first step must be a set of demands.
Many Austrian soldiers were on leave to help with the harvest. This meant that the army could not be ready to attack until about the middle of August.

On 13 July, an official whom Vienna had sent to Sarajevo reported on what he had found. He saw proof that Serbian officers had helped the plotters, but none that the Serbian government had planned the murder.
On 14 July, Tisza changed his mind and agreed to send demands to Serbia. He had been persuaded partly by the support from Germany, and Austria promised not to take any Serbian land.
The Austrians wrote their demands so harshly that Serbia could hardly accept all of them. The final text was agreed on 19 July, but it was still kept secret.
The Austrians waited to deliver the note until the French president had left Russia. They wanted to stop France and Russia from agreeing a common reply while the leaders were still together.
On 20 July, the French president, Raymond Poincaré, arrived in Russia by ship with Prime Minister Viviani. There were parades, dinners and speeches about the friendship of the two countries.
While the visitors dined with the Tsar, workers in St Petersburg went on strike in large numbers. These strikes showed that the Tsar had serious troubles at home.
In Britain, the government was busy with a bitter quarrel about Ireland that seemed close to a civil war. Most ministers had given little thought to the Balkans.
In Serbia, politicians were busy with an election campaign. They knew that Austria was angry, but they did not expect such a hard blow so soon.

At six o'clock on the evening of 23 July, Baron Giesl, the Austrian minister in Belgrade, brought the note to the Serbian foreign ministry. The prime minister was away, so the acting leaders received it.
The note was long and strict, and it contained ten separate demands. It began by saying that Serbia must publicly condemn the propaganda against Austria-Hungary and promise to end it.
Serbia had to stop newspapers that attacked Austria and close the groups that worked against it. It also had to change what was taught in schools and dismiss officers named by Vienna.
Serbia was told to arrest two men who had helped the plotters, Major Tankosić and a man named Ciganović. It must also stop the smuggling of weapons across the border.
Two of the demands worried the Serbs more than all the others. Austrian officials would work inside Serbia to end the movement, and they would take part in the investigation of the plot.
The deadline was forty-eight hours, until six o'clock on the evening of 25 July. If the answer was not good enough, Austria would end diplomatic relations.
Prince Alexander, who ruled Serbia in place of his sick father, sent a telegram to the Tsar asking for help. Other friends of Serbia were also asked for advice.
Berlin told the other powers that the quarrel was between Austria and Serbia alone. No other country, it said, had any right to interfere in the matter.
In London, Sir Edward Grey read the note and was shocked. He told the German ambassador that he had never seen such a harsh document sent by one independent state to another.
In St Petersburg, the Russian foreign minister, Sazonov, was very angry when he read the note. He is said to have told the Austrian ambassador that Austria was setting Europe on fire.
On 24 and 25 July, the Russian ministers met to decide what to do. They agreed that Russia could not let Serbia be crushed, and the army was told to begin getting ready.
In Belgrade, Pašić and his ministers worked for hours on their reply. Britain and France advised them to go as far as they possibly could to meet the Austrian demands.
On 25 July, Serbia ordered its army to be called up. The government also prepared to move out of Belgrade, which was close to the Austrian border.
On 25 July, just before the deadline at six o'clock, Pašić brought the reply to Giesl in person. The Austrian had already packed his bags and had a train ready.
Serbia's reply was polite, and it accepted almost every demand. It promised to dissolve the groups and punish the guilty if Austria could show evidence of who they were.
Serbia refused only the demand that Austrian officials should work inside Serbia, since this would break its laws. It offered to let the Hague court or the great powers decide.
Giesl said that the answer was not satisfactory, and he left Belgrade by train about half an hour later. Diplomatic relations between Austria-Hungary and Serbia were now broken off completely.

That evening, Austria ordered a partial mobilisation, which means calling up part of its army, against Serbia. The troops would still need many days, and the army could not attack before the middle of August.
In London, Grey and others who read the reply thought that Serbia had gone a very long way. They found it hard to see why Austria could not accept it.
That night, crowds gathered in Vienna and Berlin to cheer the news. In London, Paris and St Petersburg, however, people began to be afraid.
On 24 July, the British cabinet spent most of its meeting on the quarrel about Ireland. Only at the end did Sir Edward Grey read out the Austrian note to his colleagues.
Grey proposed that Britain, France, Germany and Italy should work together as mediators. These four countries were not directly involved in the quarrel between Austria and Russia.
France and Italy accepted Grey's plan, and Russia was willing to go along with it. Germany, however, refused, saying that it could not put its ally before a kind of European court.
Sazonov, the Russian foreign minister, tried to talk directly to the Austrian ambassador. But Vienna refused to change its plans, and the talks led nowhere.
Britain's fleet had gathered for a review and was due to go home. Winston Churchill, who was in charge of the navy, ordered it to stay together, and this was a quiet warning to Germany.
France wanted to know whether Britain would help it if war came. Grey could not promise anything, because his government and Parliament were divided.

Historians still ask whether a clearer British warning would have made a difference. Some think it might have made Germany more careful, while others think it might have made France and Russia bolder.
On 29 July, Grey spoke plainly to the German ambassador, Prince Lichnowsky. He said that if France was drawn into the war, Britain might not be able to stay out.
At this stage, most British ministers hoped that Britain could stay out of any war. Many people in Britain also did not see why their country should fight over a quarrel in the Balkans.
In the last days of July, shares fell sharply in many capitals. Anxious people rushed to the banks to take out their money, and some stock exchanges had to close.
On 28 July, Emperor Franz Joseph signed the declaration of war on Serbia. It was sent to Belgrade by telegram, and the first great declaration of war of the crisis had been made.
Vienna hurried partly because it wanted to stop other countries from arranging a compromise. Its army, however, could not begin to attack for another two weeks.
Kaiser Wilhelm had returned from his cruise and now read the Serbian reply for the first time. He wrote in the margin that, with this answer, every reason for war had gone.
The Kaiser suggested that Austria should occupy the Serbian capital, Belgrade, and then stop and talk. Berlin passed the idea to Vienna late that night, but Vienna was not interested.
Early on 29 July, Austrian gunboats on the river Danube fired shells at Belgrade. These were the first shots of the war, though the shelling did not do great damage.
On 29 July, Russia ordered a partial mobilisation, aimed only at Austria-Hungary. The Tsar and his ministers hoped that this would warn Vienna without threatening Germany.
The Kaiser and the Tsar were cousins, and they sent each other telegrams in English. They signed as Willy and Nicky, and each said that he wanted to save the peace.
On the evening of 29 July, the Tsar signed an order for a general mobilisation. Then, after a telegram from the Kaiser, he cancelled it in the night and kept only the partial plan.

On 29 July, Germany asked Britain to stay neutral if war broke out between the great powers. It promised not to take any French land in Europe, but it would not make the same promise about French colonies, and Britain refused.

On 30 July, the German chancellor told Vienna that Germany could not be dragged into a world war because Austria ignored its advice. On the same day, the German army chief urged the Austrians to mobilise against Russia.
On 30 July, Sazonov and the Russian generals went to the Tsar again. They argued that a partial mobilisation would not work, and that Germany seemed to be getting ready for war.
That afternoon, the Tsar reluctantly agreed and signed the order for a general mobilisation. It would be announced to the public the next morning.
Russia was a huge country with slow railways, and its army needed much longer than Germany's to get ready. For this reason, its generals wanted to begin as early as they could.
A mobilisation meant notices on walls and reservists leaving their farms and factories. Horses were taken for the army, and trains were packed with soldiers going to the border.
For Germany, the Russian mobilisation was a serious threat to its whole plan of war. Its plan depended on beating France before Russia was ready, so any Russian preparation started a clock.
The German chancellor, Bethmann Hollweg, wanted Russia to look like the first to move. He hoped that Germans, including the Socialists, would then believe in a war of defence.
General Moltke, the German army chief, believed that delay was very dangerous. He pushed for an order to mobilise at once, but the Kaiser and the chancellor still wanted to wait.
On 31 July, after news came of Russia's general mobilisation, Germany announced a state of imminent danger of war. This was a step before full mobilisation, and it allowed some preparations to begin.
On 31 July, Austria-Hungary ordered a general mobilisation of its own. It would be ready to face Russia as well as Serbia, but the first day of mobilisation would be 4 August.
By the night of 31 July, three empires were calling up soldiers. Peace now depended on whether Russia would stop within hours.
On the night of 31 July, Berlin sent Russia an ultimatum. It demanded that Russia stop all its military measures against Germany and Austria within twelve hours.

Russia gave no answer to the German ultimatum before the twelve hours were over. Its generals said that an army once called up could not easily be stopped, and that stopping would leave the country in a mess.

On the same evening, the German ambassador in Paris asked whether France would stay neutral in a war between Germany and Russia. He wanted a clear answer by one o'clock the next afternoon, which was eighteen hours away.
Earlier, France had ordered its troops to stay about ten kilometres from the border. The government wished to show that it was not the one starting the trouble.
That evening in Paris, the Socialist leader Jean Jaurès, who had worked hard for peace, was shot dead in a cafe. His killer was a young man who hated his views.
On the morning of 1 August, Viviani answered that France would act according to its own interests. By noon, the German deadline for Russia had passed in silence.
On the afternoon of 1 August, France ordered a general mobilisation. Posters went up in the streets, and the church bells rang in the villages to call the men to arms.
At five o'clock on the afternoon of 1 August, the Kaiser signed the order for general mobilisation in Germany. The great plan for war was ready to begin.

On the evening of 1 August, the German ambassador in St Petersburg handed Sazonov a declaration of war. Germany, the note said, had received no reply to its ultimatum and now considered itself at war.
That night, large crowds in Berlin cheered and sang patriotic songs. Many families, however, were afraid for their husbands and sons.
On the evening of 1 August, a message arrived from the German ambassador in London. It suggested that Britain might stay out of the war, and might keep France quiet, if Germany did not attack France.
The Kaiser was delighted by the news from London and called for his generals at once. He told General Moltke to stop the plan against France and to send the armies east to fight Russia alone.
General Moltke said that the plan could not be changed. The army had been arranged for war in the west first, and a million men could not be turned around at will.
The Kaiser was angry and disappointed, but in the end he gave way. Moltke was shaken by the argument, and the plan stayed as it was.
That night, King George V of Britain sent a message to the Kaiser, saying that there must have been a misunderstanding. Britain, it turned out, had made no firm promise about France.
On 2 August, German troops entered Luxembourg, a very small country in the west. The great powers, including Germany, had promised to respect its neutrality.
On the evening of 2 August, Germany gave Belgium an ultimatum. It demanded that Belgium let German armies pass through its land, and promised to leave after the war.
Germany said that France was planning to march through Belgium. It gave no proof, and in fact the French troops were still kept away from the border.
King Albert of Belgium and his ministers met that night to decide what to do. They knew that the Belgian army was very small beside the German one.
On the morning of 3 August, Belgium refused the German demand. It said that it would defend itself against any attack, and it asked Britain and France for help.
On Sunday, 2 August, the British cabinet met and argued for hours. Many ministers did not want war, but Grey made it clear that he could not stay in government if Britain abandoned France.
The cabinet agreed that the Royal Navy would protect the northern coast of France if the German fleet attacked it. Grey told the French ambassador about the promise later that same afternoon.
The leaders of the opposition party wrote to the prime minister, Asquith, that same day. They said that it would be a mistake for Britain to hold back from helping France and Russia.
The news of the German demands to Belgium changed British opinion quickly. In 1839, Britain and other powers had promised to protect Belgium's independence.
Britain also had practical reasons to care about Belgium. For centuries it had refused to let any strong power hold the ports across the Channel.
On Monday, 3 August, Grey spoke to the House of Commons for about an hour. He explained Britain's duty and interests, and most members cheered.
Two ministers, John Burns and John Morley, resigned because they did not want to go to war. The rest of the cabinet held together, including Lloyd George, who had doubted.
That evening, Grey stood at his window and watched the lamps being lit outside. He later remembered saying that the lamps were going out all over Europe.
On the evening of 3 August, Germany declared war on France. The German note gave false reasons, such as French air raids that had never taken place.
On the morning of 4 August, German soldiers crossed the border into Belgium. In London, the British government sent Germany an ultimatum, which would end at midnight.

On the evening of 4 August, the German chancellor met the British ambassador, Sir Edward Goschen. He said that Britain was going to war just for a scrap of paper, meaning the old treaty about Belgium.

In the German parliament, Bethmann Hollweg admitted that the invasion of Belgium was a wrong, but he said that necessity knew no law. Even the Socialists voted to give the government the money for war.
In London, the clock showed eleven o'clock, which was midnight in Berlin. No answer came from Germany, and Britain was now at war.
That night, crowds gathered outside Buckingham Palace and in the streets to sing and cheer. Yet many people also felt fear and sorrow, even if they did not show it.
At Liège, the Belgians fought hard from their forts. They slowed the German advance for days, until the Germans brought up very heavy guns that destroyed the forts.
Britain's declaration of war brought its empire in as well. Soldiers came from Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and India to help.
Italy stayed neutral at first, saying that the Triple Alliance was a defensive one. Japan soon joined the war on the side of Britain, and the Ottoman Empire joined Germany in the autumn.
Most people expected a short war that would be over by Christmas. A few leaders, such as Lord Kitchener in Britain, warned that it could last for years.
In September, the French and British stopped the German advance near the river Marne. Both sides then began to dig trenches, and neither could move forward.
The war lasted until November 1918, more than four years. Millions of soldiers and civilians were killed, and the fighting spread to many parts of the world.
By 1922, four great empires had fallen: the Russian, the German, the Austro-Hungarian and the Ottoman. New countries appeared on the map, among them a state for the South Slavs.
The peace treaty of 1919 was signed exactly five years after the murder in Sarajevo. It said that Germany and its allies were responsible for the war, and many Germans resented this deeply.
In the 1960s, the German historian Fritz Fischer argued that German leaders bore the main responsibility. Many other historians today describe a shared failure, in which every great power took risks.
Austria-Hungary decided to use the murder to deal with Serbia once and for all. It wrote a note that was hard to accept, and it declared war before its army was ready.
Germany gave Austria its blank cheque, and then it was bound by a plan that left no room for delay. When war came, it invaded neutral Belgium and brought Britain into the fight.
Other countries also made choices that made war more likely. Russia mobilised early, France backed Russia, Britain was slow to speak clearly, and Serbia could not control its secret groups.
In the crisis, leaders had little time, little trust and no easy way to pause. Each move made by one country frightened the next, and the fear then led to another move.
One lesson is that in a crisis, leaders should slow down and keep talking. After the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, the Soviet Union and the United States set up a direct line between their capitals.
Another lesson is to ask what the other side fears. In 1914, every great power believed that it was only defending itself, but each looked like a threat to its neighbours.

It took thirty days, from Germany's promise on 5 July to Britain's declaration on 4 August, for a regional crisis to become a world war. No single person wanted that result, yet choices made one after another led millions into it.
C1C2: In the summer of 1914, Europe looked like the safest and most prosperous place on Earth, with busy cities, fast new railways and holidaymakers crowding every beach. Yet beneath that calm, the great powers had spent years building armies and quietly planning for a war that all of them claimed not to want. In little more than a month, one murder in a small city would drag almost every one of them into it.

By 1914, fast trains carried families to the seaside, steamships linked the continents, and telegraph wires let a headline cross Europe in the time it took to drink a cup of coffee. Cities such as Paris, Berlin and Vienna glittered with new theatres, department stores and electric lights. It was an age of confidence, in which many people believed that progress would only continue.

Among the great powers of western and central Europe, there had been no major war since 1871, so a whole generation had grown up knowing armies mostly as parades and uniforms. Old soldiers still told stories of the battles of their youth, which younger people could hardly imagine. Peace had begun to feel normal, almost permanent, and that feeling made danger easy to overlook.

Factories, banks and shipping lines had tied the economies of Europe together, and Britain and Germany were among each other's best customers. Several well-known writers argued that a war between great powers would be so ruinous that no sensible government would ever begin one. History was about to test that comfortable idea very severely, and the answer would be painful.

Even so, every great power was spending heavily on soldiers, guns and warships, and the bills rose year after year. Each government insisted that it was only protecting itself, yet each watched its neighbours' preparations with growing alarm. In this way, defence on one side looked very much like a threat to the other.

Six states were counted as the great powers of Europe in 1914: Britain, France, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia and Italy. They were the countries whose armies, navies and diplomats decided most of what happened on the continent, and whose rulers expected small nations to listen politely. Italy was the weakest of them, and Austria-Hungary, in its own way, was nearly as fragile.

Britain and France ruled vast empires in Africa and Asia, while Germany had acquired colonies of its own and wanted a larger share. Austria-Hungary and Russia were empires of a different kind, built across land and filled with many peoples who spoke many languages. Every great power therefore had both something to protect and something to fear losing.

Many of the rulers of Europe were related by blood, and the grandchildren of Queen Victoria sat on several thrones. The Kaiser in Berlin and the Tsar in St Petersburg even wrote to each other in English, like cousins at a family party. Yet the interests of their states counted for far more than the warmth of their letters.

Cheap newspapers, school lessons and public ceremonies taught ordinary people to take fierce pride in their own nations. Unfortunately they also taught them to see other nations as rivals, and sometimes as enemies who were waiting for a moment of weakness. Leaders who might have wished to compromise knew that angry readers and voters were watching every move they made.

This book asks a simple but troubling question: how did a peaceful European summer turn into a world war in about thirty days? To find the answer we must first meet the countries, the promises and the plans that were already in place before a single shot was fired. Then we can follow, day by day, the decisions that carried everyone over the edge.

In 1871, after defeating France in a swift war, the German states were united into a single empire under the king of Prussia. The new emperor was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, right in the heart of the country that had just been beaten. Europe suddenly had a powerful new neighbour in the middle of the map, and nobody was quite sure how to deal with it.

As the price of defeat, France had been forced to hand over Alsace and a large part of Lorraine to the new German Empire. Many French people never accepted the loss, and the memory of it kept alive a quiet longing for revenge. German leaders knew this very well, and it made them suspicious of France for decades.

Otto von Bismarck, the German chancellor, believed that the new empire could remain safe only if France stayed isolated. With great skill he wove agreements with other great powers so that no country would be willing to stand beside the French. For twenty years his careful diplomacy kept the peace, but it depended on the cleverness of one man.

In 1879, Germany and Austria-Hungary signed a treaty promising to support each other if either were attacked by Russia. Italy joined them three years later, and the three countries became known together as the Triple Alliance. At first it seemed a sensible way to keep the peace, since everyone would think twice before attacking such a strong group.

Wilhelm II became German emperor in 1888, at the age of twenty-nine, and he was proud, restless and eager to make his own mark. In 1890 he dismissed Bismarck, and soon Germany let its secret agreement with Russia lapse. The careful balance that the old chancellor had built over so many years began to fall apart.

Russia, no longer tied to Berlin by treaty, turned towards France, which badly wanted a friend, and in the 1890s the two made a military alliance. Each promised to come to the other's help if Germany attacked, which meant that Germany now faced possible enemies on two sides. French money poured into Russian railways, and the two armies began to make plans together.

For many years Britain had preferred to stand apart from the alliances of the continent, relying on its navy and its empire. In 1904, however, it settled its old colonial quarrels with France, and in 1907 it did the same with Russia. These friendly understandings, known as the Entente, were not treaties of war, but they drew Britain steadily into the French and Russian camp.

Officially, Britain had promised nothing, and its ministers told Parliament that its hands were free. Yet from 1906 British officers held secret talks with their French colleagues about how the two armies and navies might work together, and over the years those plans took on a life of their own. A promise that was never written down could still become a moral debt, and a hard one to refuse.

By 1914, Europe had divided into two armed camps, with Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy on one side and France, Russia and Britain on the other. The system was meant to prevent war by making every attack look dangerous, yet it also meant that a quarrel between any two countries could quickly drag in all the others. The web of promises protected Europe only for as long as no strand of it was pulled.

Italy belonged to the Triple Alliance on paper, but it was easily the least reliable member of the three. It still dreamed of gaining Trento and Trieste, towns with many Italian speakers that lay inside Austria-Hungary, so it could hardly be called a true friend of Vienna. The alliance was also purely defensive, which would matter a great deal when war came.

In France, Germany, Russia and Austria-Hungary, young men were required to serve in the army for a period and then return to civilian life as reservists. In an emergency, those millions of trained men could be called back to their regiments within days. Armies on this scale could be raised only by great organisation, and that organisation set its own rules.

Kaiser Wilhelm dreamed of a navy that would match Germany's growing wealth, and his admiral, Alfred von Tirpitz, set about building one with great energy. Britain, whose trade and safety depended entirely on the sea, saw a German fleet in the North Sea as a direct challenge to its position. Within a few years the two nations were locked in a race to build bigger ships.

In 1906, Britain launched HMS Dreadnought, a battleship so heavily armed and so fast that older warships suddenly looked obsolete. Every navy that wished to be taken seriously now had to build such ships, and the race began again from the start. For Germany, whose industry was strong, it was a chance to catch up, which made the British more anxious still.

Battleships were enormously expensive, and both countries paid for them with higher taxes and political quarrels. The race did not give Germany the sea power it had hoped for, because Britain simply built more, but it did teach many British people to distrust German motives. A rivalry that nobody had really needed to have was now firmly established in both countries.

Twice, in 1905 and again in 1911, Germany challenged French influence in Morocco in an attempt to prove that it could not be ignored. In the second crisis it sent a gunboat, the Panther, to the port of Agadir, and for some weeks war seemed possible. Each time, the result was the opposite of what Germany wanted, since Britain drew closer to France.

Many Germans felt that their country was surrounded, with France to the west, Russia to the east and the Royal Navy controlling the seas beyond. German leaders worried that time was against them, and that their rivals would grow too strong to be resisted if they waited too long. This anxiety, not simple greed, helps to explain some of the risks they were willing to take.

In 1905, Russia was defeated by Japan, and a wave of strikes and protests shook the empire. Over the next years, helped by French loans, it rebuilt its army and laid new railways towards its western frontier. German generals looked at those lines and the long-term numbers and began to wonder whether Russia would soon be too strong to resist.

General Alfred von Schlieffen, who led the German general staff until 1906, spent years planning for a war against France and Russia at once. His idea was to defeat France in a few weeks by a great sweep through Belgium, before the slower Russian army could be fully ready. The plan needed speed above all, and it left no easy way to fight just one enemy.

Every great power had written detailed railway timetables for carrying millions of men and their horses and guns to the frontier. These plans were prepared years in advance, with every train, bridge and station counted, and officers practised them in peacetime again and again. The system worked wonderfully well, but it was designed to be started, not stopped.
