All the armies' plans rested on the same assumption: that whoever moved first and fastest would win, and that the war would be short. In that logic, any delay seemed a dangerous mistake, and any pause for talking seemed a gift to the enemy. The generals were not wicked, but they had built a machine that rewarded haste, and politicians would soon find it hard to slow down.

The Balkans are the mountainous lands of south-east Europe, where many peoples, languages and religions meet. For centuries most of them had belonged to the Ottoman Empire, but by 1914 that great empire was weak and shrinking. Its decline left a dangerous space, and every ambitious neighbour wondered who would fill it.

During the nineteenth century, Greeks, Serbs, Romanians, Bulgarians and other peoples won their freedom from Ottoman rule, often after bitter wars and uprisings. Serbia, which had governed itself in part for decades, was recognised as fully independent in 1878 at a congress of the great powers in Berlin. Each new country was proud, poor and ambitious, and each wanted more land than it could easily win.

Many of the peoples of the Balkans, including the Serbs, are Slavs, and most of them belong to the Orthodox Church. Russia, the largest Slav country, liked to present itself as their natural protector, and Russian public opinion often demanded that the government help them. Serbia, for its part, learned to look to St Petersburg whenever it was in trouble.

Many Serbs dreamed of a single state that would unite all the South Slavs, meaning the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes who spoke closely related languages. The difficulty was that millions of those people lived inside Austria-Hungary, so the dream was in effect a plan to take pieces of the Habsburg empire. Vienna understood that very well, and from then on it watched every move that Belgrade made with deep suspicion.

Austria-Hungary was a patchwork of peoples, among them Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Croats, Serbs, Romanians and Italians, with two capitals in Vienna and Budapest. Its emperor, Franz Joseph, had ruled since 1848 and had come to seem as permanent as the mountains. In 1914 he was eighty-three, and many people wondered quietly what would happen when he died.

Many of the peoples inside Austria-Hungary wanted more rights, and some wanted to leave altogether. The authorities in Vienna feared that an independent and successful Serbia would act like a magnet for the empire's own Slav subjects, drawing them away. They therefore saw Serbian nationalism not as a quarrel across the border, but as a danger to their survival.

Austria-Hungary had occupied Bosnia since 1878, and in 1908 it formally annexed the province, which many Serbs had hoped to see join Serbia. Belgrade was furious, and Russia protested, but with Germany standing firmly behind Vienna the Russians had to back down. The humiliation was not forgotten in St Petersburg, and it made Russia less willing to give way again.

In 1912, Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro joined forces against the Ottoman Empire and drove it out of nearly all its land in Europe. The winners then quarrelled over the spoils and fought each other in a second war in 1913, from which Serbia emerged much larger and more confident. Its army had proved itself, and its leaders began to dream of what might come next.

In 1913, with Austrian support, the great powers helped to create a new country, Albania, partly to prevent Serbia from reaching the Adriatic Sea. When Serbian troops stayed on in the north of the new country, Vienna sent a sharp warning in October, and Serbia withdrew. That success may have convinced some Austrian leaders that firm threats against Serbia could work again.

Inside Serbia, patriotic societies and some army officers quietly trained and helped young men who wished to resist Austrian rule in Bosnia. Prime Minister Nikola Pašić and his government, exhausted after two wars, mostly wanted peace, but they could not fully control these networks. Exactly how much the government knew, and when, is still argued about by historians.

Franz Ferdinand had not been born expecting to inherit the throne of Austria-Hungary, and for many years it seemed unlikely that he ever would. He became the heir only after the death of his cousin Rudolf, the emperor's son, in 1889, and then the death of his own father in 1896. By 1914 he was fifty years old, and he had spent two decades preparing, impatiently, for the day when the old emperor would be gone.

In 1900, Franz Ferdinand married Countess Sophie Chotek, whom he loved deeply, against the wishes of the emperor and the court. Because her family was not royal enough by the strict rules of the Habsburgs, their children could never inherit the throne. At court, Sophie was often made to walk behind the other archduchesses, which both she and her husband found very painful.

At home in Konopiště castle, in Bohemia, the couple lived quietly and happily with their three children, far from the cold formalities of Vienna. The archduke could be stern and quick to anger in public, but he was a devoted father and a passionate gardener who built a famous rose garden. Even the Kaiser came to admire the roses there in June 1914, only about two weeks before the murder.

Franz Ferdinand believed that the empire could survive only if it gave its Slav peoples a larger voice, and he made plans for reforms once he was on the throne. Many Hungarian leaders hated the idea, since it would reduce their own power, while some Serb nationalists feared that it might make Habsburg rule too attractive to Slavs. He was therefore distrusted on more than one side, and he had few real friends at court.

In earlier Balkan crises, a number of generals and ministers had urged war against Serbia, but Franz Ferdinand usually argued against it. He feared that a war would unleash forces that might destroy the empire and bring Russia into the fight. In a bitter irony, the plot against him would remove one of the most cautious people in Vienna.

The Black Hand was a secret society of Serbian officers, founded in 1911 and led by a colonel called Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, who wished to bring all Serbs together. In Bosnia, a group of young students and workers called Young Bosnia admired earlier rebels, such as Bogdan Žerajić, who in 1910 had tried to shoot the Austrian governor. Neither group was the same as the Serbian government, but their members knew each other.

In June 1914, the archduke travelled to Bosnia to watch army exercises, and he planned to end his trip with a visit to Sarajevo on 28 June. That date is St Vitus's Day, or Vidovdan, which Serbs remember as the anniversary of their defeat by the Ottomans at Kosovo in 1389. Because the archduke came as an inspector of the army, Sophie could ride beside him in public, which court rules rarely allowed.

Gavrilo Princip was born in 1894 into a poor Serb farming family in the hills of Bosnia, and he was a thin, serious young man who loved poetry and politics. He was a good student who left school in Sarajevo and went to Belgrade in 1912, where he joined other young nationalists in their cafes. At nineteen, he burned with the belief that Bosnia must be free of Austrian rule.

In the spring of 1914, Princip and two friends in Belgrade, Nedeljko Čabrinović and Trifko Grabež, decided to kill the archduke when he visited Bosnia. Men connected with the Serbian army, including a major called Vojislav Tankosić, supplied them with pistols and bombs and taught them to shoot. Historians still argue about how far the plot was known to leaders such as Apis, and whether the government in Belgrade knew anything at all.

In the weeks before the visit, the young men crossed into Bosnia with their weapons hidden, helped along a smugglers' route by border guards. In Sarajevo, a young man named Danilo Ilić gathered more helpers, until seven conspirators were ready to act on 28 June. Nobody in the Austrian government yet suspected them, and only a few Serbian officials may have heard even a vague warning of trouble ahead.

On the warm and sunny morning of 28 June 1914, the archduke and his wife Sophie travelled by train from the spa town of Ilidža into the city of Sarajevo. The streets had been decorated with flags and carpets, and many people had come out to catch a glimpse of the visitors. Franz Ferdinand wore a general's uniform with a hat of green feathers, and the mood, at least on the surface, was cheerful.

A procession of six cars set off along the main road beside the river, with the mayor and the chief of police leading the way. The archduke's open car came second, with its roof folded back so that the crowds could see the royal couple clearly. It was a courteous gesture, but it also made them very easy to see for anyone who meant them harm.

Seven young men had taken up their places in the crowd at different points along the river road, each carrying a bomb or a pistol. They had arranged themselves so that if one of them failed, the next might still have his chance. It was a clumsy plan, put together by boys with little training, but it needed only a single success.

As the archduke's car rolled past the first two conspirators, nothing happened at all. According to accounts given later, one of them lost his nerve at the decisive moment, and another found that a policeman was standing too close to act. For a few minutes it looked as though the whole plot might fail without a shot being fired.

Near a stone bridge, at about ten past ten, Nedeljko Čabrinović struck the cap of his bomb and hurled it at the archduke's open car. It bounced off the folded roof and rolled into the road, where it exploded under the car behind and wounded several officers and some people in the crowd. The archduke himself was not hurt, although some accounts say that he knocked the bomb away with his arm.

Čabrinović swallowed a pill of poison and jumped over the wall into the river below, hoping to die rather than be captured. The poison was old and only made him ill, and the river was so low in the summer heat that he was easily seized by the police. He was dragged out and beaten by an angry crowd before he was taken away.

The rest of the cars sped on to the Town Hall, where the mayor stood ready to give his speech of welcome. The archduke, pale with shock and anger, told him sharply that he had come as a guest and had been greeted with bombs. After a moment, however, he calmed himself, and the long official speeches went on as if nothing had happened.

After the speeches, the archduke decided to give up the rest of the programme and visit the wounded officers in the hospital instead. Sophie, who had been shaken but not injured, chose to go with him, and nobody seems to have believed that a second attack was possible. To avoid the crowded old town, the plan was to drive straight along the river road.

Nobody had properly told the driver of the second car about the change of route, and when the cars reached the corner he followed the original plan and turned right into a narrow side street. The governor, Oskar Potiorek, called out that this was the wrong way, and the driver braked and began to back the heavy car out. For a few fateful moments it stood almost motionless in the narrow street, directly in front of the corner.

By a stroke of chance that has been remembered ever since, Gavrilo Princip was standing outside a small delicatessen near the corner, only a few steps from the stopped car. He had heard the first bomb explode earlier, and now the same car had returned and stopped almost in front of him. He saw the royal couple sitting there in the sunshine, stepped forward without a word, and drew his pistol from his coat.

From only a few steps away, Princip fired twice into the open car, and the sound of the shots was lost in the noise of the street. One bullet struck the archduke in the neck and the other hit Sophie in the body, though for a moment both of them sat upright, and few people understood what had happened. The driver sped away towards the governor's residence, with the royal couple slumped in their seats.

The archduke and his wife were carried into the governor's residence, where doctors tried in vain to help them. Within a short time, both had died of their wounds, Sophie almost at once and her husband only a little later. Their three children were far away in Bohemia, and would soon learn that they had lost both their parents.

Princip tried to turn the pistol on himself, and he also swallowed the poison he carried, but both attempts failed. Bystanders and police seized him at once, and he was beaten before he was taken away. Like Čabrinović, he had hoped to die for his cause, and now he would have to answer for it.

The police questioned the two prisoners, and within days most of the other plotters had been found and arrested. The investigators learned that the bombs had been made in a Serbian army workshop and that the young men had been helped across the border by Serbian officials. What they could not yet prove was whether the leaders of the Serbian government had known about the plan.

That evening and throughout the following day, angry crowds in Sarajevo attacked the shops and houses of local Serbs, who were widely blamed for the murder. For many hours the authorities did little to stop the violence, and it took a long time before order was restored. The first victims of the crime were therefore ordinary people who had nothing to do with it.

Emperor Franz Joseph was at his summer villa in the mountain town of Bad Ischl when the telegram reached him. He had already lost a son, a brother and a wife to tragedy, and he was shaken by the murder, though he had never been close to his nephew. The old man was now being asked, once again, to take on a heavy decision.

Kaiser Wilhelm was at the Kiel sailing regatta, on the Baltic coast of Germany, when the news reached him. He was deeply upset, because he had known the archduke and liked him, and he abandoned the races to return to Berlin. In the days that followed, he began to think that this was a moment for Austria to settle accounts with Serbia once and for all.

Across Europe, flags were flown at half mast, and kings and presidents sent messages of sympathy to Vienna. Most newspapers described the murder as a terrible crime, but few of their readers feared that it would lead to a war between the great powers. After all, there had been assassinations before, and the crises in the Balkans had always been solved in the end.

The funeral in Vienna took place in the first days of July, and it was much plainer than the burial of a future emperor would usually have been. The court was still upholding the old rule that Sophie, who was not of royal blood, could not lie in the family vault, so the couple were buried together at Artstetten castle. Many people at the time felt that the plain ceremony was a final slight against a woman who had been slighted all her life.

The Serbian government declared that it condemned the crime and would punish any of its subjects who were found to be guilty. But some newspapers in Belgrade wrote with open bitterness about Austria, and a few seemed to take a quiet pleasure in the news, which angered the officials in Vienna still more. In both capitals, public feeling was becoming a force that ministers could not easily ignore.

General Conrad von Hötzendorf, the chief of the Austrian army staff, had called for war against Serbia on many earlier occasions. The old emperor had always refused, but now the murder of the heir gave Conrad his strongest argument yet. He warned that if Austria did nothing again, its enemies would draw the obvious conclusion about its weakness.

Count Leopold Berchtold, the foreign minister, was by nature cautious and had a reputation for avoiding hard decisions. This time he became convinced that the empire must show real strength against Serbia, or else lose its standing as a great power in the eyes of the world. Having reached that view, he pursued it with a determination that surprised many of his colleagues.

Many in Vienna feared that if they did nothing, Austria-Hungary would look weak in front of Serbia, its own peoples and the other powers. For a great power of that age, a loss of respect, which they called prestige, seemed almost as dangerous as a lost battle. The empire was old and creaking, and its leaders were afraid that one more humiliation might finish it.

Count István Tisza, the prime minister of Hungary, was the strongest opponent of a quick attack on Serbia, and his voice mattered because Hungary shared the government of the empire. He feared that a war might bring Russia and Romania into the fight, and that conquering more Serbs would only add to the empire's unhappy Slav population. He insisted that any move should at least begin with a firm diplomatic demand.

The Austrians knew perfectly well that Russia might defend Serbia, and their own army was not strong enough to face both at once. They could not risk a war against Serbia unless Germany promised to stand behind them, and Germany was their only truly reliable friend. Everything therefore depended on what Berlin would say, and on how quickly it would say it.

Emperor Franz Joseph wrote a personal letter to Kaiser Wilhelm, and a long paper on Balkan policy was added to it. The paper had been drafted before the murder, and it had been rewritten afterwards to argue that Serbia must be weakened as a political power. The letter did not say exactly what Austria planned to do, but its meaning was clear to anyone who read it.

Count Alexander Hoyos, a young diplomat and one of Berchtold's closest aides, was chosen to carry the letter to Berlin in person. He left Vienna by train on 4 July with the papers in a leather case, and he understood that he was carrying the empire's future in his hands. In Berlin, he was to explain what Austria wanted, and to find out what Germany would say.

On 5 July, the Austrian ambassador, Count Szőgyény, handed the letter to Kaiser Wilhelm at the New Palace in Potsdam, near Berlin. The Kaiser read it carefully, and then said that he would give his full answer only after he had talked with his Chancellor. Even so, he told the ambassador that Austria could count on Germany's faithful support.

Meanwhile, Count Hoyos talked with senior officials of the German foreign office, who were just as supportive as the Kaiser had been. Some of them added that Austria should act quickly, while the sympathy of Europe was still with it, if it meant to act at all. The message travelled back to Vienna that evening, and it was warmer than the Austrians had dared to hope.

In Berlin, many officials hoped that Austria would strike swiftly at Serbia, while Europe was still shocked by the murder, so that the war would stay small and local. They also knew perfectly well that Russia might join in, and that the danger would then be much greater. It was a gamble, and it was made with open eyes by men who understood what they might lose.

On 6 July, the German chancellor, Theobald von Bethmann Hollweg, met the Austrian visitors and confirmed the promise that the Kaiser had made the day before. He told them that Austria must decide for itself what to do about Serbia, and that it would be wise not to wait too long. It was an offer of complete support, with no questions asked and no conditions attached to it.

Berlin did not ask what Austria planned to demand from Serbia, nor how far it intended to go, and it did not see the actual terms until shortly before they were sent. Historians have since called the promise a blank cheque, because it allowed Vienna to fill in any amount it chose. A cheque of that kind can be written only by a country that is ready to pay.

Germany had few reliable friends in Europe, and Austria-Hungary was by far the most important of them. German leaders feared that if Berlin refused to help now, Vienna might lose confidence, look for new partners, or even collapse under the weight of its quarrels. Seen from Berlin, supporting Austria was therefore a way of protecting Germany itself, not just a favour to a friend.

German leaders hoped that the Tsar would not wish to be seen defending the assassins of an archduke, since the murder had been committed by men who attacked monarchy itself. They also hoped that Russia, which was still rebuilding its army, would shrink from a war. It was an understandable hope, but it rested on guesses about the feelings of other people.

Historians still disagree about how far German leaders actually expected, or even wished for, a wider war. Some believe that they hoped for a small local conflict, while others believe that they were prepared to risk a general war, partly because they thought it would be easier to win soon than later. What is clear is that they did not rule a bigger war out, even though they hoped to avoid one.

Some German officers believed that Russia was growing stronger every year, thanks to its new railways, its larger army and its rapidly growing industry. They argued that if war had to come anyway, it would be safer to fight in 1914 than three years later, when Russia would be better prepared. Not every leader shared this view, but it influenced many of those who did.

On 6 July, Kaiser Wilhelm set off on his usual summer cruise to the fjords of Norway, and several other senior officials and officers also went on leave. Some historians think that this was meant to show the world that nothing unusual was going on, while others think it simply shows how little the leaders expected a world war. Either way, the sense of quiet that spread across Europe that month was deeply misleading, as events would soon show.

Neither Austria nor Germany told Italy, their partner in the Triple Alliance, what was being prepared. The Italian government would learn about the plan only when events had gone so far that it could not have any influence over them. It was a small example of the secrecy that would make the crisis harder to manage.

With the promise from Berlin in its pocket, Vienna was free to choose its own course. At the same time, however, Germany had tied its own fate to whatever Austria decided to do next, and it had lost much of its power to steer. A friend who promises everything in advance gives away the right to say no later on.

After 6 July, almost nothing seemed to happen in public, and for more than two weeks the newspapers carried little worrying news. Behind closed doors, however, the Austrian government was drafting its demands for Serbia, and it was in no hurry to show them. The thirty days that would change the world, and so many lives, had in fact begun in near silence.

On 7 July, the Austrian ministers met in Vienna to decide on their course of action. Most of them wanted to strike at Serbia without delay, but Tisza, whose agreement was essential, insisted that the first step must be a set of firm demands. Several ministers hoped privately that Serbia would refuse, and that war would then follow.

In the countryside, many Austrian and Hungarian soldiers were on leave to help bring in the harvest, and calling them back would take time. The army's own plans meant that it could not be ready to attack Serbia in strength until about the middle of August. The government therefore had weeks in which to prepare its demands and its diplomacy.

On 13 July, an official whom Vienna had sent to Sarajevo reported on what the investigation had discovered so far. He found evidence that the plot had been prepared in Belgrade and that Serbian officers and border guards had helped the plotters, but no proof that the Serbian government had planned or even known about the murder. The finding was awkward for those who wanted to place the blame on Serbia as a state.

By 14 July, Tisza had changed his mind and agreed that demands should be sent to Serbia, partly because he had been persuaded by Germany's firm support and by the fear that the empire would look weak. The ministers agreed to declare that Austria did not intend to take any Serbian land, a promise meant to reassure Russia. With the Hungarian prime minister at last on board, the way was open for the next stage of the plan.

The Austrians wrote the demands in such harsh terms that Serbia, as an independent country, could hardly be expected to accept every one of them. The final text was approved at a meeting of ministers on 19 July, yet the world was told nothing and the document was kept strictly secret. Some of those who wrote it seem to have wanted a refusal, because a refusal would give Austria the war it was looking for.

Vienna decided to deliver the note only after the French president, Raymond Poincaré, had finished his visit to Russia. The Austrians wanted to avoid giving the French and Russian leaders the chance to agree on a common response while they were still sitting at the same table. The delay produced the delivery date of 23 July, and the thirty days gathered pace from there.

On 20 July, President Poincaré arrived in Russia by warship, accompanied by the French prime minister, René Viviani, for a long-planned state visit. There were military parades, glittering dinners and warm speeches about the strength of the alliance between the two countries. Behind the ceremonies, the Russians and French spoke seriously about the Balkans and what they would do if trouble came.

While the visitors were dining with the Tsar, thousands of workers in St Petersburg were out on strike, and there were angry clashes with the police. The unrest was a reminder that the Russian empire had serious troubles of its own and that its government was not as secure as it looked. Some leaders in Germany may have hoped that these troubles would make Russia cautious.

In Britain, the government was absorbed in a bitter quarrel about the future of Ireland, which many people feared might lead to civil war. A conference at Buckingham Palace tried to find a solution that week, and most ministers had given hardly any thought to the Balkans. It is remarkable how a great crisis can arrive while attention is turned somewhere else.

In Serbia, many politicians were busy with an election campaign, and the prime minister, Pašić, spent part of the month away from the capital. They knew that Austria was angry and might demand something, but they did not expect a hard blow so soon after the murder. Belgrade was about to be given the shortest of warnings, and the quietest weeks of that summer were nearly over.

At six o'clock on the evening of 23 July, Baron Giesl, the Austrian minister in Belgrade, climbed the steps of the Serbian foreign ministry with a sealed note in his hand. The prime minister, Pašić, was away on his election tour, so the acting ministers had to receive it. Giesl said that he expected an answer in two days, and then he left.

The note listed ten demands, and it opened with the requirement that Serbia must publicly condemn all propaganda against Austria-Hungary and promise to put an end to it. It then spoke about the murder in sharp terms, and suggested that Serbian officials had been careless or worse. Everything about its tone made clear that Vienna was no longer in a mood to bargain.

Serbia was told to suppress newspapers that attacked Austria-Hungary and to dissolve the patriotic societies that worked against it. It was also required to change what was taught in its schools and to dismiss officers and officials whose names Vienna would supply. Each demand on its own might have been debated, but together they looked like a list of conditions that a defeated country might expect.

Serbia was ordered to arrest Major Tankosić and a railway official named Milan Ciganović, the two men who had helped the young plotters, and to stop the smuggling of weapons across the border. The border officials who had helped the conspirators to cross were to be punished as well. These demands were fair in themselves, since the men were clearly connected to the plot.

Two of the demands troubled the Serbs more than all the rest, because Austrian officials would be allowed to work inside Serbia to suppress the movement against Austria and to share in the investigation of the plot. To most Serbs this looked like a loss of independence, and they could not easily imagine a government that would agree to it. Whether Vienna intended that effect, or simply wanted a refusal, is still part of the argument among historians.

The note gave Serbia only forty-eight hours to reply, which meant that the answer was due at six o'clock in the evening on 25 July. If the answer was not good enough, Giesl had been told to break off diplomatic relations and leave, an action that in those days often came before a war. It was the kind of deadline that left little room for talking, or for asking friends to help.

Prince Alexander, who governed Serbia as regent for his sick father, sent a telegram to the Tsar in which he explained that Serbia could not defend itself and appealed for Russian help. Serbian diplomats also asked Britain and France for advice and support, and many telegrams went out that night from Belgrade. The little country had never felt so alone, and so dependent on the decisions of great men far away.

Berlin quickly sent a message to the other great powers, saying that the quarrel was a matter between Austria-Hungary and Serbia alone and that no other country should interfere. It added that any interference would risk consequences that nobody would be able to control. In London and St Petersburg, the message was read as a warning, not as an invitation to talk.

In London, Sir Edward Grey read the note on 24 July and was shocked at its tone and at its short deadline. He told the German ambassador that he had never before seen one independent state send another a document of so forceful a kind. Yet he also said that a quarrel between Austria and Serbia alone was not Britain's business, though he feared that Russia would be drawn in.

In St Petersburg, the Russian foreign minister, Sazonov, was furious when he read the note, and he is said to have told the Austrian ambassador that Austria was setting Europe on fire. Russia asked Vienna to extend the deadline so that other powers could study the evidence, but the request was refused. The French leaders, still at sea on their way home from Russia, could only follow events by wireless and telegram.

On 24 and 25 July, the Russian ministers met, with the Tsar present on the second day, to decide how to answer the Austrian note. They agreed that Russia could not stand aside and watch Serbia be crushed, and the army was ordered to start certain preparations for war. Nobody in the room called these steps a mobilisation, but others would see them as the first move.

In Belgrade, Pašić returned from his campaign and led his ministers through long hours of work on a reply that was both polite and careful. The British and French governments advised them to go as far as they possibly could to meet the Austrian demands, while Russia urged them not to fight if they were attacked. The Serbs knew that the whole world would read every word they wrote, and weigh it carefully.

On the afternoon of 25 July, before they had even delivered their reply, the Serbs ordered their army to mobilise. The government also prepared to leave Belgrade, which lay almost on the Austrian border and could be struck at once, and it moved the same night to the town of Niš. The Serbs had decided that they would give way as much as they could, but that they would not be caught unprepared.

At about ten minutes to six on 25 July, only a short time before the deadline, Prime Minister Pašić brought the Serbian reply to Giesl in person. The Austrian diplomat had already packed his bags, and he had a carriage and a train waiting, because he had been told to leave if the answer was not a full acceptance. He glanced through the paper quickly and said that it was not enough to satisfy his government.

The Serbian reply was written in courteous language, and it accepted almost every one of the demands in some form. It promised to ban the hostile publications, dissolve the societies, dismiss the officers named by Vienna and punish those who had helped the plot, so long as Austria supplied evidence. Many people who read it afterwards thought that it went further than any independent state could be expected to go.

Serbia refused only a part of the demands, the proposal that Austrian officials should take part in the inquiry and in the suppression of subversion inside Serbia, because that would violate its laws and its independence. It offered instead to let the international court at The Hague, or the great powers, decide any questions that remained. It was a way of saying that Serbia would bend, but would not break.

Giesl declared that the answer was not satisfactory, because it was not an unconditional acceptance, and he left Belgrade by train about half an hour later. He crossed the river to Austrian territory, and diplomatic relations between Austria-Hungary and Serbia were broken. In many wars of that age, such a step was the one that came just before the guns.

That same evening, Austria ordered a partial mobilisation against Serbia, which meant calling up part of its army, not all of it. The troops would still need many days before they were ready to attack, and Austria had left its forces on the Russian border alone, hoping that Russia would stay out. It was a small decision that would prove to be a very big one.

In London, Sir Edward Grey and the other ministers who read the Serbian reply thought that Serbia had gone a very long way towards meeting the Austrian demands. They found it hard to see why Austria could not at least accept it as the basis of talks. The reply did a great deal to shape British sympathies in the days that followed.

That night, crowds gathered in Vienna and Berlin to sing patriotic songs and to cheer the news that Austria had broken with Serbia. In London, Paris and St Petersburg, ministers and officials were reading the same telegrams with growing dread. Two days had passed since the note was delivered, and almost every country now felt that it was being pushed towards a decision.

On 24 July, the British cabinet spent most of its meeting on the dispute about Ireland, which seemed far more urgent than anything in the Balkans. Only at the end did Sir Edward Grey read the Austrian note to his colleagues, and the ministers listened with growing seriousness. It was the first time that most of them had thought about the crisis as a danger to Britain.

Grey proposed that the four powers not directly involved, Britain, France, Germany and Italy, should work together as mediators between Austria and Russia. He suggested that their ambassadors should meet in London to find a way out before the fighting started. It was a sensible idea, and it had worked during the Balkan crisis of the year before.

France and Italy accepted Grey's plan, and Russia indicated that it was willing to go along with it. Germany, however, refused on 27 July, saying that a meeting of that kind would amount to a European court in which Austria would be put on trial. Berlin preferred that Austria and Russia talk directly, a way of dealing with things that Austria was not eager to accept either.

Sazonov, the Russian foreign minister, tried hard to find a compromise in direct conversations with the Austrian ambassador in St Petersburg. But Vienna was determined not to change its course, and it refused to discuss the terms of its note with anyone but the Serbs. For a few anxious days the talks continued, but they made no real progress towards a settlement.

Britain's great fleet had gathered at Portland for a test mobilisation and a royal review, and in the last days of July it was due to disperse to its home ports. Winston Churchill, the First Lord of the Admiralty, quietly ordered the ships to stay together at full strength, which was a warning to Germany that did not need to be spoken aloud. Soon afterwards the ships steamed north towards their wartime base in Scotland, as quietly as such a great fleet can move.

France wanted to know whether Britain would stand beside it if war came, and the French ambassador in London pressed Grey hard for an answer. Grey could not give a promise, since his own cabinet was divided and Parliament had never been asked to approve any commitment to fight. Britain's silence left both its friends and its rivals uncertain about what it would do.

Historians still ask whether a clearer British warning, given early, might have changed the outcome of the crisis. Some argue that it would have made Germany more careful, while others reply that it could just as easily have made France and Russia bolder, and that a divided cabinet could not have given such a warning anyway. The question cannot be settled, but it shows how much depended on what leaders left unsaid.

On 29 July, Grey spoke more plainly than before to the German ambassador, Prince Lichnowsky, who had himself been urging Berlin to be careful. He said that if the war spread and France was drawn in, Britain might not be able to stand aside. Lichnowsky sent the warning to Berlin that same day, where it was read with irritation and alarm.

At this stage, most members of the British cabinet still hoped that Britain could stay out of a continental war, and many ordinary people saw no reason why their country should fight over a quarrel in the Balkans. Public opinion was far from ready, and a government that tried to lead the country into war too early would probably have lost its majority. That is why the events of the following days, and the way in which they were presented, would matter so much.

In the last days of July, share prices fell sharply in many European capitals, and anxious people queued at banks to withdraw their savings in gold coins. Several stock exchanges closed their doors, because nobody knew what anything was worth if war came. Businessmen, who had said for years that war would be too costly, now watched their fears become real.

On the morning of 28 July, Emperor Franz Joseph signed the declaration of war on Serbia at Bad Ischl, and in the middle of the day it was sent to Belgrade by telegram. It was the first declaration of war of the crisis, exactly one month after the murder in Sarajevo. At eighty-three, he was signing the order that would, in the end, bring down his empire.

Vienna was in a hurry partly because it wanted to prevent the other powers from arranging a compromise that would leave its demands unsatisfied. In reality the Austrian army could not begin to attack Serbia for nearly another two weeks, so the declaration was more a political signal than a military order. The war therefore began on paper long before it began in the field, and nobody could now call it back.

Kaiser Wilhelm had cut short his cruise and was back in Germany, and on 28 July he read the Serbian reply for the first time. He was impressed, and he wrote in the margin that, with such an answer, every reason for war had fallen away. His view was that the demands had been met well enough for Austria to stop and talk.

The Kaiser suggested that Austria should occupy the Serbian capital, Belgrade, as a pledge, and then halt and negotiate from a position of strength. Berlin passed the idea on to Vienna late that night, but the Austrians were reluctant to stop, having just declared war, and they did not take it up. A chance to slow the machine down was offered that night, and it was not accepted by those who held the levers.

Early on 29 July, Austrian gunboats on the Danube opened fire on Belgrade, which lay on the river just across the border. These were the first shots of the war, though the shelling was limited and did little harm. In Russia, the news made it harder than ever for the government to remain calm.

On 29 July, Russia ordered a partial mobilisation of its army, directed only against Austria-Hungary. The Tsar and his ministers hoped that this would warn Vienna to stop without seeming to threaten Germany, which was Austria's ally. Unfortunately, many Russian generals thought that a partial plan was impractical, and some of them warned that it would make a general mobilisation harder.

The Kaiser and the Tsar, who were related, exchanged a series of telegrams written in English and signed with their family names, Willy and Nicky. Each one declared that he wanted to save the peace, and each one pointed to the other's military measures as the greatest obstacle. The messages sometimes crossed on the wires, so that each man answered something that had already been overtaken.

On the evening of 29 July, after much pressure from his ministers, the Tsar signed an order for a general mobilisation against both Austria and Germany. Later that night, after a telegram from the Kaiser, he changed his mind and cancelled it, keeping only the partial plan against Austria. It showed how heavily the decision weighed on a man who wished sincerely to avoid war.

On 29 July, the German chancellor asked Britain to remain neutral in the event of a war, promising that Germany would not take any French land in Europe. He would not make the same promise about French colonies, and Grey replied the next day that Britain could not accept a bargain that would leave France at Germany's mercy. The offer was refused, and London began to look at Berlin with deeper suspicion.

On 30 July, the German chancellor Bethmann Hollweg, alarmed by Grey's warning, told Vienna several times that Germany could not be dragged into a world war because Austria ignored its advice. On the very same day, the German army chief Moltke sent a message urging the Austrian army chief to mobilise against Russia at once and promising Germany's support. The civilians in Berlin and the generals were now pulling in opposite directions, and the Austrians could choose whichever message suited them.

On 30 July, Sazonov and the Russian generals went to the Tsar once more, and they argued with great urgency. A partial mobilisation, they said, was not workable and would spoil the plans for a larger one, and Germany seemed to be getting ready for war anyway. The Tsar, who had hoped that the telegrams between cousins would keep the peace, was greatly troubled.

That afternoon, after a long struggle with himself, the Tsar reluctantly signed the order for a general mobilisation of the whole Russian army. It would be announced to the public the next morning, and from that moment, Russia was committed to a path that it could not easily leave. Even then, the Russians insisted that mobilisation did not mean war, and the Tsar repeated that he wished for peace.

Russia was a vast country with a thin network of railways, and its army needed far longer than Germany's to assemble on the frontier. For this reason the Russian generals wanted to begin as early as possible, and they feared that every day of delay would leave their country dangerously weak. From their point of view, too much caution was the greatest risk of all, since a slow start could mean defeat.

A mobilisation meant that notices were nailed to walls and doors, and that millions of reservists left their farms and factories to join their regiments. Horses were taken for the army and trains were packed with soldiers going towards the border, often in the middle of the harvest. It was not yet a war, but to anyone who watched, it looked very much like the first act of one.

For Germany, the Russian mobilisation was a very serious threat, because its whole plan depended on defeating France before Russia could bring its great army to bear. Any Russian preparation therefore started a clock, and German generals began to say that every hour mattered. They did not stop to ask whether Russia might only be trying to deter Austria.

The German chancellor, Bethmann Hollweg, was careful to wait until Russia appeared to be the first to move. He hoped that if the Russians began, many Germans, including the powerful Socialist party, would believe that the war was one of defence. He also hoped that Britain, which was watching closely, would not blame Germany for starting a war.

General Moltke, the head of the German army, argued with real passion that every hour of delay put the country in danger. He pressed the chancellor and the Kaiser for an order to mobilise at once, and he was supported by the minister of war. For a short time, the civilians held out, but the news from Russia was making their position harder.

On 31 July, after news arrived of Russia's general mobilisation, Germany declared a state of imminent danger of war, which was the step just before full mobilisation. It allowed the army to take certain measures, and it told the whole world that the moment of decision was close. In Berlin, crowds gathered in the streets to read the news and to wait for more.

On 31 July, Austria-Hungary ordered a general mobilisation of the whole army, which meant that it would face Russia as well as Serbia. The first day of the mobilisation would be 4 August, and the army's plans for Serbia and for Russia had to be fitted together in great haste. The decision made war with Russia far more likely, and it did little to help Austria against Serbia.

By the end of 31 July, Russia and Austria-Hungary were mobilising, and Germany was on the verge of doing so. The timetables were now in charge, and they allowed very little room for argument or doubt. Peace depended on whether the Russians could be persuaded to stop within hours, which in practice seemed very unlikely.

On the night of 31 July, Berlin sent Russia an ultimatum, which the German ambassador delivered in St Petersburg around midnight. It demanded that Russia stop all its military measures against Germany and Austria-Hungary within twelve hours, or Germany would mobilise. It was a demand that the Russian government, with its army already moving, could hardly have met even if it had wanted to.

Russia did not send any answer to the German ultimatum before the time limit ran out. Its generals insisted that an army once called up could not be stopped without chaos, and the Tsar's government had no wish to undo the one thing that might protect Russia in a war. The twelve hours passed, and the silence from St Petersburg seemed to Berlin to prove its worst suspicions.

On the same evening, the German ambassador in Paris called on the French prime minister, René Viviani, and asked whether France would remain neutral in a war between Germany and Russia. He demanded an answer within eighteen hours, and, according to the instructions that Berlin had prepared, he was ready to ask for French border fortresses as a pledge if the answer was yes. No French government, whatever its politics, could have accepted such a price and survived.

Two days earlier, the French government had ordered its troops to stay about ten kilometres back from the German frontier, a decision that its general staff disliked intensely. The ministers wanted the whole world, and Britain in particular, to see that France was not the one starting the trouble. General Joffre protested that every day of delay would cost France dearly in a war.

That same evening in Paris, the Socialist leader Jean Jaurès, who had campaigned tirelessly for peace between France and Germany, was shot dead as he sat at a cafe table. His killer, a young nationalist, was angry at the speeches he had made against war. The news shook the city, and it removed from French politics the most famous voice that might have opposed the coming war.

On the morning of 1 August, Viviani gave the German ambassador his answer, which was that France would act according to its own interests. At noon, the German deadline for Russia ran out without any reply from St Petersburg. The two ultimatums had done the work that Berlin's planners expected, and the machinery of war was now almost impossible to stop.

On the afternoon of 1 August, the French government ordered a general mobilisation of its army, although the order was careful to say that mobilisation was not war. Posters were pasted up on walls across the country, and church bells rang in the villages to call men to their regiments. In the fields, farmers laid down their tools in the middle of the harvest and went home to pack.

At five o'clock on the afternoon of 1 August, Kaiser Wilhelm signed the order for general mobilisation in Germany, only a short time after France had ordered its own. The great railway timetables, planned over many years, were now to be put into operation. For German officers, it was the moment for which they had prepared throughout their careers.

On the evening of 1 August, the German ambassador in St Petersburg, Count Pourtalès, handed Sazonov a declaration of war on behalf of the Kaiser. Germany, he said, had received no reply to its ultimatum, and so it considered itself at war with Russia. The scene was a painful one, and it is said that the ambassador was close to tears as he left.

That evening, large crowds gathered in the centre of Berlin to cheer and sing patriotic songs, and similar scenes took place in many other German cities. Behind the flags and the music, however, many families were quietly anxious about their husbands and sons. Even the Socialists, who had held big peace meetings only days before, were now deciding how to respond to the war.

On the evening of 1 August, a message arrived from Prince Lichnowsky, the German ambassador in London, who had spoken with Sir Edward Grey. It seemed to suggest that Britain might stay out of the war and might even keep France quiet, so long as Germany did not attack France. Lichnowsky had understood Grey too hopefully, but in Berlin the news was read with great relief.

The Kaiser was delighted by the news, and he turned at once to General Moltke with a new order. The army, he said, should stop the plan against France and march east to fight Russia alone, leaving France and Britain out of the war. In a single evening, it seemed that a world war might be avoided after all.

General Moltke replied that this was quite impossible, since the German army and its railway timetables had been arranged for years to strike against France first. He said that an army of a million men could not be turned around in an afternoon, and that if the Kaiser tried to do it, he would get a confused crowd instead of an army. His argument rested on the plan, not on any wish for war, but the plan itself had become a kind of fate.

The Kaiser was angry and bitterly disappointed, and he told Moltke that he had expected a different answer from the chief of the army. But after some time he gave way, and Moltke, who was greatly shaken by the quarrel, left the room with the plan unchanged. It is an example of how an army's schedule had become the master of the leaders who were supposed to control it.

Later that night, King George V of Britain sent a message to his cousin the Kaiser, saying that there must have been some misunderstanding about a friendly conversation. Britain, it turned out, had made no firm promise about keeping France out of the war. The hope that had lit up the evening in Berlin was gone almost as quickly as it had come.

On 2 August, German troops entered the tiny Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, which lay on the way to France and whose neutrality had been guaranteed by the great powers in 1867. The Germans said that they needed to protect the railways there, and the small country could do nothing to stop them. It was a first sign that they did not intend to let a treaty stand in their way.

On the evening of 2 August, the German minister in Brussels handed the Belgian government an ultimatum demanding that German armies be allowed to pass freely through Belgium. Germany promised to withdraw after the war and to pay for any damage, but if Belgium refused, it would be treated as an enemy. Belgium was given only twelve hours to answer, and the deadline fell at seven o'clock the next morning.

In the ultimatum, the German government claimed that France was planning to march through Belgium, so that Germany would have to get there first. It offered no proof, and in fact French troops had been ordered to stay well back from the border. The claim was a way of covering what had always been the central idea of the German plan.

King Albert of Belgium and his ministers met in the royal palace that night to decide what to do. They knew very well that their army was small beside the huge German one, and that to refuse might mean the ruin of their country. They also knew that to give way would mean surrendering their independence without a single shot.

On the morning of 3 August, Belgium gave its answer, which was that it refused the German demand and would defend itself against any attack. The government described the German proposal as a violation of international law, and it appealed to Britain and France for their help. A small country had made a great decision, and now the world would watch what the others did.

On Sunday, 2 August, the British cabinet met twice and argued for hours about what Britain should do. Many ministers hoped to stay out of the war, but Grey made it clear that he could not remain in the government if Britain abandoned France. The meeting ended without a decision to fight, though it did reach a limited agreement.

The cabinet did agree that if the German fleet came into the English Channel or attacked the northern coast of France, the Royal Navy would protect it. Grey passed on this promise to the French ambassador, Paul Cambon, in the afternoon, and the promise was limited, though it was real. It was not yet a promise of war on land, but it was far more than Britain had said before.

That same day, the leaders of the Conservative opposition, Bonar Law and Lord Lansdowne, wrote to the prime minister, Asquith. They said that it would be a mistake and a danger for Britain to hold back from supporting France and Russia, and that they would stand behind the government. The letter showed that a divided Liberal cabinet might still be able to lead a united country.

The news of the German ultimatum to Belgium changed British public opinion very quickly indeed, and it did so almost overnight. In 1839, Britain and the other great powers had signed a treaty in which they promised to protect Belgium's independence and neutrality, and for many people the treaty now stood for something larger. A small, peaceful country was being threatened by a powerful neighbour, and that was an argument that ordinary people could understand.

Britain also had hard, practical reasons to care about the fate of Belgium, quite apart from any question of honour. For centuries, its governments had refused to let any strong power control the Belgian and Dutch coast, which lay only a short way from the mouth of the Thames. Honour and interest therefore pointed in the same direction, and it was hard to say which carried more weight in the minds of ministers.

On Monday, 3 August, which was a bank holiday, Sir Edward Grey stood up in the crowded House of Commons and spoke for about an hour. He told the members about the talks of the previous days, about Britain's duty to Belgium and about its own interests, and he told them of Belgium's appeal for help. When he sat down, most of the House cheered, and it was clear that the government could count on a large majority.

Two ministers, John Burns and John Morley, resigned from the government because they could not support a war. The rest of the cabinet held together, including David Lloyd George, who had been one of the doubters until the news from Belgium made up his mind. The prime minister, Asquith, had managed to keep his divided government in one piece.

That evening, as the lamps were being lit in the streets outside, Grey stood with a friend at the window of his office in the Foreign Office. He later remembered saying that the lamps were going out all over Europe, and that they would not be lit again in the lifetime of those who were looking. His words have become among the most famous ever spoken about the start of the war.

On the evening of 3 August, the German ambassador in Paris handed the French government a declaration of war. The German note gave reasons that turned out to be false, such as the claim that French aeroplanes had dropped bombs on German cities and that French troops had crossed the border. In truth, Germany was acting on a plan that had been made years before.

On the morning of 4 August, German soldiers crossed the frontier into Belgium, and the neutral country was invaded. In London, the British government demanded that Germany promise to respect Belgian neutrality, and it sent an ultimatum which would expire at midnight, Berlin time. Everything now depended on whether Berlin would pull back, and almost nobody believed that it would.

On the evening of 4 August, the German chancellor met the British ambassador, Sir Edward Goschen, in an emotional interview. According to Goschen, Bethmann Hollweg said that Britain was going to war against a kindred nation just for a scrap of paper, by which he meant the old treaty about Belgium. To the British, the words showed how little Germany understood what a promise meant to them.

In the German parliament that day, Bethmann Hollweg admitted that the invasion of Belgium was a wrong, but he claimed that necessity knew no law, and that the wrong would be made good when the war was won. Even the Socialists, who had opposed war so loudly a week earlier, voted to give the government the money for it. The Kaiser declared on the same day that he no longer saw parties among his people, only Germans.

In London, the clock struck eleven, which was midnight in Berlin, and the British ultimatum ran out. No answer had come from Germany, and so Britain was now at war, and the order to begin hostilities was sent out to the fleet. A few ministers sat in silence at their table in Downing Street, as the tension of the last days drained out of the room.

That night, large crowds gathered outside Buckingham Palace and in the streets of London to sing patriotic songs and to cheer the King. Yet many people felt a quiet fear and sorrow beneath the excitement, and there were also some who thought that the war was a terrible mistake. Similar scenes of noisy excitement mixed with private worry could be found in Paris, Berlin, Vienna and St Petersburg.

At Liège, the Belgian soldiers fought hard from their forts, and the Germans lost many men in their first attacks. The small army slowed the German advance for several days, until the Germans brought up enormous guns that could smash the forts one by one. The delay gave the French and British a little time, though not as much as they would have liked.

Britain's declaration of war brought its whole empire into the conflict, and the other countries of the empire gave their support. In the months and years that followed, soldiers and workers came from Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and India, as well as from many other lands. For the first time, a quarrel that began in the Balkans was being fought on every continent.

Italy declared itself neutral, saying that the Triple Alliance was a defensive one and that Austria had started the quarrel, and it stayed out until it joined the other side in 1915. Japan entered the war against Germany in August, and the Ottoman Empire joined Germany and Austria-Hungary in the autumn. Austria declared war on Russia on 6 August, which meant that all the great powers except Italy were now at war.

Most people, both soldiers and civilians, expected a short war that would be over by Christmas, and young men worried that they might miss it. A few leaders, among them Lord Kitchener, the new British minister of war, warned that it could last for years and would need millions of men. The history of the next four years would show, in the most painful way, how right he was.

In September, the French and British armies stopped the German advance near the river Marne, so Germany's plan for a quick victory failed. Both sides then dug into the ground to protect themselves from the new, deadly weapons, and neither could break through. Before the year ended, a line of trenches stretched for hundreds of kilometres from the North Sea to Switzerland.

The war lasted until November 1918, more than four years after it began, and it became one of the deadliest in history. Estimates vary, but about nine million soldiers were killed, along with millions of civilians who died from fighting, hunger and disease. The great armies that had cheered on their departure had found something that none of their plans had prepared them for.

By 1922, four great empires had fallen, the Russian, the German, the Austro-Hungarian and the Ottoman, and the map of Europe had been redrawn. New countries appeared, among them a state for the South Slavs that was later called Yugoslavia, and the old empires of the east were gone for ever. The world that the leaders of July 1914 had tried so hard to preserve had been swept away by the war they had failed to prevent.

The peace treaty of 1919 was signed at Versailles on 28 June, exactly five years after the murder in Sarajevo. One of its clauses placed responsibility for the war on Germany and its allies, and it was used to justify heavy payments for the damage. Many Germans deeply resented the clause, and the argument about it poisoned politics for years.

In the 1960s, the German historian Fritz Fischer argued that Germany's leaders bore the main responsibility for the war, and his claim caused a storm of argument. Many other historians today describe instead a shared failure, in which leaders in several capitals took risks that they did not fully understand. Each new set of documents adds something to the picture, which is why the debate has never really ended.

Austria-Hungary decided to use the murder to settle its quarrel with Serbia once and for all, and it aimed at a small war while accepting the risk of a larger one. It wrote a note that was meant to be hard to accept, and it declared war before its own army was ready to fight. Its leaders believed that they were defending the empire, but their actions helped to destroy it.

Germany gave Austria a blank cheque, and then it found itself bound by a plan that left no room for delay or for any change of mind. When the moment of decision arrived, its army invaded neutral Belgium, which brought Britain into the war and turned a European conflict into a world one. A plan made to protect Germany had in effect forced its leaders to take the very step that most endangered it.

Other countries made choices that also made war more likely, some of them out of fear and some out of loyalty. Russia mobilised early, France gave its ally strong backing, Britain was slow to speak clearly, and Serbia could not or would not control the secret groups that worked against Austria. In each case the leaders could point to good reasons, which is exactly why the story is so hard to judge.

In the crisis, the leaders had little time, little trust in one another and no easy way to pause. Every move made by one country frightened the next, and the fear then produced another move, in a chain that moved faster than the telegrams could carry messages of peace. Many of the men involved were intelligent and decent, but they were making huge decisions while exhausted and afraid.

One lesson of these thirty days is that in a crisis, leaders should slow down, keep talking and keep as many options open as they can, since a deadline can turn into a trap. After the dangerous Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, the Soviet Union and the United States set up a direct line of communication between their capitals, so that messages could travel in minutes instead of hours. It was a small and practical answer to one of the great problems of 1914.

Another lesson is to ask what the other side fears, for in 1914 every great power believed that it was only defending itself, and every one of them looked like a threat to its neighbours. Mobilisation, plans for speed and promises of support all seemed sensible from the inside, and all seemed menacing from the outside. A leader who can see his own actions through the eyes of his rival has a better chance of avoiding a war that nobody really wants.

It took thirty days, from Germany's promise to Austria on 5 July to Britain's declaration of war on 4 August, for a quarrel in the Balkans to become a war that spanned the world. Nobody planned it that way, and nobody seems to have wanted that outcome, yet each decision, taken by tired people in rooms far from the front, made the next one harder to refuse. That is the lasting warning of these thirty days: wars can arrive not through one great blunder but through many small steps.
